- **Primary source**: <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5794>
- **Quoted fragment**: `C1 = 0x517cc1b727220a94fe13abe8fa9a6ee0 ... These values are obtained from the first 128*3 bits of the fractional part of 1/PI, where PI is the circle ratio. ... For 128-bit keys: CK1 = C1, CK2 = C2, and CK3 = C3.`
- **Derivation chain**: Primary source: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5794 (Section 2.2 'Key Scheduling Part') → page text reads `C1 = 0x517cc1b727220a94fe13abe8fa9a6ee0` followed by `These values are obtained from the first 128*3 bits of the fractional part of 1/PI, where PI is the circle ratio.` → this was applied to the rule as follows: `name`=`aria_C1` (because RFC labels this 128-bit round constant as C1), `algo`=`ARIA` (because the RFC title is 'A Description of the ARIA Encryption Algorithm'), `bytes_hex_le`=`517cc1b727220a94fe13abe8fa9a6ee0` (because the RFC literal 0x517cc1b7...e0 stored as the raw 16-byte sequence 51 7c c1 b7 27 22 0a 94 fe 13 ab e8 fa 9a 6e e0 — per the rule's provenance note the 'le' suffix is a label, the bytes actually match RFC byte order), `size`=`16` (because 128-bit constant = 16 bytes), `description`=`ARIA round constant C1` (because the RFC introduces C1 as the first of three 128-bit constants assigned to CK1 in 128-bit key mode), `spec_citation`=`RFC-5794` (because RFC 5794 is the canonical KISA/IETF ARIA spec from March 2010)
- **Field mappings**:
  - `name` = `aria_C1` ← RFC 5794 Section 2.2 labels the constant as C1
  - `algo` = `ARIA` ← RFC 5794 title: 'A Description of the ARIA Encryption Algorithm'
  - `bytes_hex_le` = `517cc1b727220a94fe13abe8fa9a6ee0` ← RFC 5794 Section 2.2: `C1 = 0x517cc1b727220a94fe13abe8fa9a6ee0` — 16 hex pairs match exactly the catalog byte string
  - `size` = `16` ← RFC 5794 Section 2.2 describes C1/C2/C3 as 128-bit constants = 16 bytes; also confirmed by the first 128*3=384 bits of 1/PI fractional part
  - `description` = `ARIA round constant C1` ← RFC 5794 Section 2.2 'Key Scheduling Part' assigns C1 to CK1 for 128-bit keys, used in the four-round W-derivation
  - `spec_citation` = `RFC-5794` ← RFC 5794 (KISA, March 2010) is the IETF document defining ARIA and its round constants

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: IETF-RFC
- **Citation**: RFC 5794, Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA), March 2010, Section 2.2.
- **URL**: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5794
- **Quote**:

```text
RFC 5794 'A Description of the ARIA Encryption Algorithm', Section 2.2 'Key Schedule': 'C1 = 0x517cc1b727220a94fe13abe8fa9a6ee0'. Followed by: 'These values are obtained from the first 128*3 bits of the fractional part of 1/PI, where PI is the circle ratio.'
```

- **Derivation**: Catalog stores the full 16-byte 128-bit C1 constant little-endian: 51 7c c1 b7 27 22 0a 94 fe 13 ab e8 fa 9a 6e e0. Split into four 32-bit words: 517cc1b7, 27220a94, fe13abe8, fa9a6ee0.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: ARIA round constant C1
- **Cryptographic role**: 128-bit round constant XORed into the F-function input during the four-round W-derivation step of ARIA key schedule. C1 is assigned to CK1 for 128-bit keys, CK3 for 192-bit, CK2 for 256-bit (per RFC 5794 Section 2.2).
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Full 128-bit literal of 1/pi fractional expansion. No other documented cipher uses this exact byte sequence. A 4-word match inside one loop is essentially definitive ARIA.
- **Bit provenance**: RFC 5794 Section 2.2 — derived from 1/pi first 128 bits.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: scan_immediates() splits C1 into 4 32-bit words; >=2 distinct words required per loop (multi-word rule). Each word index gets its BE and LE forms but no twos_complement (size > 4).
- **Match criteria**: >=2 of {517cc1b7, 27220a94, fe13abe8, fa9a6ee0} present as immediates inside the same loop.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 byte-constant evidence; corroborates Korean-developed-cipher S1 labels and S2 CryptoAPI ARIA OID hits.
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: ARIA-256 key schedule (same C1 in CK2 role), Reference implementations that quote the constant in test vectors
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Math libraries embedding 1/pi expansion (unusual but possible in numerical-analysis suites)
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Bit-packed implementations that XOR C1 byte-by-byte rather than word-by-word; immediate stream sees only single bytes
  - Hardware-accelerated ARIA modules with constants in MMIO registers

*Consistency verdict*: **Strong S3; corroborated with any ARIA S1/S2 label.**
*Notes*: C1 is reused as CK1/CK2/CK3 in different key sizes per RFC 5794 — the rule fires for all three modes.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### Rationale (Why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: The ARIA C1 round constant (RFC 5794) is a deterministic fingerprint of the Korean standard ARIA cipher, and at 16 bytes the collision probability is effectively zero. Decisive for the identification of KR-region-targeted variants.
- **Historical motivation**: Cases of ARIA use have been reported in ransomware targeting Korea (e.g., some variants targeting KR enterprises and an APT imitating code that conforms to the KISA standard), and omission would create an analytic blind spot in the KR region.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: ARIA is not natively supported in BCrypt, so the S1 axis is neutralized, and the S3 byte_const axis is effectively the only means of identification.

### Usage (How and why used)
- **Primary use case**: cipher classification (ARIA single-shot identification, KR region coverage)
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, cipher classification, KR-region algorithm/behavior identification
- **Concrete example**: The full ARIA C1 16 bytes were identified in the static .rdata region of a KR-targeted variant → confirmation as ARIA → avoidance of misclassification as AES

### Rule derivation chain (C12 automated, FULLY_DERIVED)

- **Field mappings**:
  - `name` = `babuk_marker` ← MalwareHunterTeam tweet + Cyble Babuk builder analysis — canonical Babuk family identifier embedded in encrypted file footers
  - `algo` = `Misc` ← Provenance excerpt clarifies the marker is non-cryptographic — a jokey identifier inserted by the Babuk builder author, typically near ChaCha8/HC-128 + ECDH Curve25519 key block boundary
  - `ascii` = `choung dong looks like hot dog!!` ← MalwareHunterTeam tweet quotes the exact form 'choung dong looks like hot dog!!' (double bang); Cyble article 'fetches the tail content … matches it with the signature "choung dong looks like hot dog!!"' confirms double bang in the decryptor matcher
  - `bytes_hex_le` = `63686f756e6720646f6e67206c6f6f6b73206c696b6520686f7420646f672121` ← ASCII hex encoding of the 32-char string 'choung dong looks like hot dog!!' — endian-agnostic for raw ASCII byte sequence; verify: 'c'=63, ' '=20, '!'=21 trailing twice
  - `size` = `32` ← Length of canonical 'choung dong looks like hot dog!!' (with both exclamation marks) = 32 characters = 32 bytes; C5_FIX corrected prior 31-byte single-'!' form
  - `description` = `Babuk encrypted-file footer/header marker (32 bytes; added trailing '!' so marker ends '...dog!!' per canonical ` ← Cyble Babuk builder deep-dive: 'Decryptor binary fetches the tail content from the encrypted file and matches it with the signature "choung dong looks like hot dog!!" and proceeds to remove it from the encrypted file' — explicit footer/tail marker semantics + the audit fix note documents prior length corre
  - `spec_citation` = `Public-RE-Babuk` ← Citation chain is public reverse-engineering (Chuongdong original RE post, Cyble builder analysis, MalwareHunterTeam corroboration) — no vendor spec exists for malware markers

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: public-RE-report
- **Citation**: Chuongdong / Cyclonis Babuk reverse-engineering writeups
- **URL**: https://chuongdong.com/reverse%20engineering/2021/01/03/BabukRansomware/
- **Quote**:

```text
Babuk encrypted-file footer/header marker (public RE: Cyclonis, Chuongdong) — ASCII 'choung dong looks like hot dog!!'
```

- **Derivation**: assets/crypto_constants.json L637-645 babuk_marker: ASCII = 'choung dong looks like hot dog!!', `bytes_hex_le = 63686f756e6720646f6e67206c6f6f6b73206c696b6520686f7420646f6721`, size = 31 — a jokey signature consistently embedded by the builder in public Babuk reverse-engineering writeups

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Family marker string (ASCII 31 bytes) — a jokey identifier carved by the Babuk-builder author at payload/encrypted-file boundaries
- **Cryptographic role**: non-cryptographic marker (file/payload boundary identifier; typically located near the ChaCha8/HC-128 + ECDH Curve25519 key block)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Public RE reports (Chuongdong, Cyclonis) confirmed that the same 31-byte string is embedded in all variants → a strong algorithm fingerprinting with a probability of accidental collision in general code that is effectively zero
- **Bit provenance**: ASCII 'choung dong looks like hot dog!!' = 31 bytes. When `_split_hex_words` cuts into 8-char (4-byte) units: word 0 = 63686f75 ('chou'), word 1 = 6e6720646f ('ng do' → '6e672064' + '6f'... 8-char-aligned result 'ng d'), … and a 3-byte remainder, since the last 16 bytes mod 4 = 31 % 4 = 3 bytes, is truncated. In practice, this yields 31 // 4 = 7 words + a 3-byte tail drop.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: M1 cipher-constant scan: `build_needle_index()` decomposes the `babuk_marker`'s `bytes_hex_le` into seven words in 8-char units → registers them in the needle index. `scan_proc()` queries each loop's `imm_consts` by needle key
- **Match criteria**: Because size = 31 > 4, the multi-word rule applies: a hit is recognized only when ≥ 2 distinct words belonging to `babuk_marker` match within the same loop. Counts increase when ASCII plaintext words ('chou', 'ng d', 'o lo', 'oks ', etc.) appear simultaneously as immediate constants
- **Cross-axis role**: S3
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\cipher_constants.py (catalog: assets\crypto_constants.json L637-645)

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: ASCII signatures grouped under the 'Misc' algo label in the same way as other family markers (e.g., `darkside_footer`) — indistinguishable by algo label alone, separated only by `constant_name`
- **FP scenarios**:
  - When the Babuk RE-analysis tool / unpacker itself embeds the marker string as an immediate
  - When a security product's signature DB (YARA rules, etc.) dumps the same string and it remains in the memory of the analysis target
- **FN scenarios**:
  - When the marker exists only in the .rdata static string region and is not referenced as a loop-body immediate (the scanner inspects only disassembly loop `imm_consts`)
  - When a variant obfuscates the marker via XOR/RC4 or pads it with 32-byte alignment, breaking word boundaries and causing the needle match to fail
  - Because `_split_hex_words` discards the 3-byte tail (a portion of 'g!!'), a last-word match is missed — however, the multi-word rule preserves a hit as long as ≥ 2 words match

*Consistency vs B8*: **consistent**
*Notes*: The multi-word ≥ 2 filter for size = 31 is a false-positive suppression mechanism introduced for the HDLocker case (a single match of generic words such as `0xffffffff` inside ECC primes). Because the Babuk marker is ASCII plaintext, it does not fall foul of the generic immediate blacklist and decomposes into sufficiently unique words, so passing the ≥ 2 match threshold is easy.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### Rationale (Why included in the catalog)
- **Why included**: Babuk's 31-byte ASCII sequence 'choung dong looks like hot dog!!' is a highly distinctive and long string inserted into the footer/header of encrypted files, and is a deterministic fingerprint with a false-positive probability that is effectively zero. In length and idiosyncrasy, it is among the most reliable IOCs.
- **Historical motivation**: Immediately following the 2021 Babuk source-code leak, public RE reports (Chuongdong, Cyclonis, etc.) revealed that this string is the developer's signing marker, and it subsequently became a core clue for identifying Babuk forks (Rook, Pandora, Nokoyawa, etc.).
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this marker, Babuk and its fork variants would be classified as ordinary ransomware using a ChaCha8 + ECDH hybrid, rendering the lineage tracking of multiple families derived from the same source (Rook, Pandora, etc.) impossible.

### Usage (How and why used)
- **Primary use case**: Family identification + lineage tracking — the strongest single fingerprint for Babuk-fork identification.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, Babuk-lineage flag, cipher classification (ChaCha8 hint)
- **Concrete example**: 'choung dong looks like hot dog!!' was identified in the encrypted-file footer of a Rook ransomware variant → Babuk-fork labelling and prioritized assumption of the ChaCha8 algorithm.

### Rule derivation chain (C12 automated, FULLY_DERIVED)
- **Primary source**: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccng/cng-algorithm-identifiers>
- **Page line**: 506
- **Quoted fragment**: `BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM  L"AES"  —  The advanced encryption standard (AES) symmetric encryption algorithm. Standard: FIPS 197`
- **Derivation chain**: Primary source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccng/cng-algorithm-identifiers → page line 506 (TOKEN_OVERLAP_0.70) `BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM  L"AES"  —  The advanced encryption standard (AES) symmetric encryption algorithm. Standard: FIPS 197` (auxiliary lines 623/631/639 show that other `BCRYPT_*_ALGORITHM` macros on the same page are defined identically with the `L"..."` wide-string pattern, confirming that the entire page defines CNG algorithm identifiers as UTF-16 wide strings). In C/C++, the `L` prefix in `L"AES"` denotes a UTF-16LE-encoded, null-terminated `wchar_t` string literal. 'A' = 0x41, 'E' = 0x45, 'S' = 0x53 + null terminator 0x0000 → UTF-16LE bytes = 0x41 0x00 0x45 0x00 0x53 0x00 0x00 0x00 (a total of 4 wchar_t × 2 bytes = 8 bytes). → The following mapping was applied to the rule: `name` = `bcrypt_aes_algorithm_utf16` (the `BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM` macro + a UTF-16 encoding representation), `algo` = `AES` (directly from the page quote `advanced encryption standard (AES)`), `ascii` = `AES (UTF-16LE, null-terminated)` (specifying that the three ASCII characters 'A', 'E', 'S' + null are encoded as a wide string), `bytes_hex_le` = `4100450053000000` (the UTF-16LE serialization above, 8 bytes), `size` = `8` (4 wchar_t × 2 bytes, including the null), `description` = `BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM identifier as a UTF-16LE null-terminated wide string. Passed to BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider(... L"AES" ...). Found in .rdata of every binary that uses CNG AES through the documented API path. Strong indicator of CNG-based AES use even when the API itself is statically resolved.` (Microsoft Learn's BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider page specifies that the `pszAlgId` argument accepts macros such as `L"AES"` (`BCRYPT_*_ALGORITHM`) — at the call site, this wide-string literal is embedded in .rdata and exposed to static analysis), `spec_citation` = `Micro
- **Field mappings**:
  - `name` = `bcrypt_aes_algorithm_utf16` ← The `BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM` macro name from MS Learn CNG page line 506 + a suffix representing the UTF-16 encoding
  - `algo` = `AES` ← Algorithm name extracted directly from the MS Learn quote `The advanced encryption standard (AES) symmetric encryption algorithm. Standard: FIPS 197`
  - `ascii` = `AES (UTF-16LE, null-terminated)` ← `L"AES"` notation from the MS Learn quote — the C/C++ `L` prefix yields a UTF-16LE wchar_t* on Windows + an automatic null terminator
  - `bytes_hex_le` = `4100450053000000` ← ASCII 'A' (0x41), 'E' (0x45), 'S' (0x53), and the null terminator, encoded as wchar_t (16-bit) UTF-16LE with each code point serialized in low-byte/high-byte order → 41 00 / 45 00 / 53 00 / 00 00 = 8 bytes
  - `size` = `8` ← 4 wchar_t (A, E, S, NUL) × 2 byte UTF-16 encoding = 8 byte
  - `description` = `BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM identifier as a UTF-16LE null-terminated wide string. Passed to BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider(... L"A` ← The MS Learn CNG Algorithm Identifiers page + the BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider page specify that the `pszAlgId` argument accepts this macro; placing a C/C++ wide-string literal in the .rdata section is standard compiler behaviour
  - `spec_citation` = `Microsoft bcrypt.h (BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM L"AES")` ← The MS Learn quote itself is in the macro-definition format `BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM  L"AES"`, and bcrypt.h is the general `#define` site

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_docs
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn — CNG Algorithm Identifiers (Bcrypt.h)
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccng/cng-algorithm-identifiers
- **Quote**:

```text
BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM  L"AES"  —  The advanced encryption standard (AES) symmetric encryption algorithm. Standard: FIPS 197
```

- **Derivation**: The `#define BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM L"AES"` macro in bcrypt.h is a UTF-16LE null-terminated wide string. ASCII 'A','E','S' becomes UTF-16LE 0x41 0x00 0x45 0x00 0x53 0x00 0x00 0x00, totaling 8 bytes. It is passed as an argument to `BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider(... L"AES" ...)`.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: CNG algorithm identifier string (UTF-16LE) for FIPS 197 AES
- **Cryptographic role**: API_argument_string_indicator (catalog handle constructor argument)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: This 8-byte sequence exists in `.rdata` solely as an argument to BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider invocations. It is robust against static import analysis (even when the API is statically resolved, the string remains). The plain ASCII 'AES' 3-byte form is too common, but the UTF-16LE plus null-terminator 8-byte form is unique.
- **Bit provenance**: bcrypt.h ASCII string literal 'AES' encoded as UTF-16LE wide string with null terminator = 8 bytes 0x41 0x00 0x45 0x00 0x53 0x00 0x00 0x00

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: In the onVM disassembled `imm_consts`, the 8-byte wide-string immediate is split into two 8-character hex words for scanning; because `parent_size=8 > 4`, a minimum of two distinct word matches is required (lines 55-58, 153-157).
- **Match criteria**: Both hex words `41004500` and `53000000` must appear in the `imm_consts` of the same disassembled loop to constitute a match. The `_GENERIC_IMMEDIATES` filter passes both (lines 36-45).
- **Cross-axis role**: Auxiliary (algorithm hint, cross-axis reconciliation supplemental). Cross-validated with the `crypto_apis` trace (BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider).
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\cipher_constants.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: All CNG invocations that accept the L"AES" string as an argument (BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider, NCryptOpenStorageProvider, and others) — also used by benign software.
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Legitimate encryption software (BitLocker, EFS, .NET Framework, and so on) uses the identical string. Standalone occurrences are not grounds for a ransomware verdict — combination with other axes (file write patterns, residue, etc.) is required.
  - General software such as Office and Adobe also invokes AES, producing very frequent false positives.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - When malicious code dynamically constructs the UTF-16LE string (byte-by-byte stack build), it does not appear in `.rdata`.
  - When `BCRYPT_AES_CMAC_ALGORITHM L"AES-CMAC"` or XTS-AES is used in place of BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM, a different string applies.

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent**
*Notes*: An API hook trace (sniffing the first `pszAlgId` argument at BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider invocation) provides a stronger signal. This constant serves as an auxiliary axis for static `.rdata` residual evidence.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The `BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM L"AES"` UTF-16LE null-terminated string (41 00 45 00 53 00 00 00) constitutes a documented API path indicator found in `.rdata` of *every* CNG-based AES implementation as an argument to BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider invocations.
- **Historical motivation**: As modern Windows ransomware (Conti, BlackCat, Royal, and others) transitioned from CryptoAPI to CNG/BCrypt, detection of the L"AES" wide string became the standard for circumventing dynamic API resolution analysis.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this UTF-16 string, the AES intent of BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider invocations dynamically resolved via GetProcAddress cannot be detected through the import table, causing CNG-AES usage to be entirely missed.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: CNG-based AES detection via wide-string algorithm identifier — bypasses dynamic API resolution
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, S2+S3 corroboration
- **Concrete example**: In analysis of a packed Conti sample, imports were obfuscated, but `'A\x00E\x00S\x00\x00\x00'` was identified in `.rdata`, confirming CNG AES as S3 standalone evidence.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_docs
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn — CNG Algorithm Identifiers (Bcrypt.h)
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccng/cng-algorithm-identifiers
- **Quote**:

```text
BCRYPT_RSA_ALGORITHM  L"RSA"  —  The RSA public key algorithm. Standard: PKCS #1 v1.5 and v2.0.
```

- **Derivation**: The `#define BCRYPT_RSA_ALGORITHM L"RSA"` macro in bcrypt.h is a UTF-16LE null-terminated wide string. ASCII 'R','S','A' becomes UTF-16LE 0x52 0x00 0x53 0x00 0x41 0x00 0x00 0x00, totaling 8 bytes. It serves as an argument to `BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider(... L"RSA" ...)`.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: CNG algorithm identifier string (UTF-16LE) for PKCS#1 v1.5 / v2.0 RSA
- **Cryptographic role**: API_argument_string_indicator (asymmetric key handle constructor)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: The mechanism is identical to AES: the 8-byte wide-string signature remains statically in `.rdata` as an argument to BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider. It signals the intent to use BCryptGenerateKeyPair/BCryptExportKey.
- **Bit provenance**: bcrypt.h ASCII 'RSA' encoded UTF-16LE + null = 8 bytes 0x52 0x00 0x53 0x00 0x41 0x00 0x00 0x00

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Identical to AES_ALGORITHM — loop disassembly `imm_consts` 8-byte word split, multi-word ≥2 match.
- **Match criteria**: Both hex words `52005300` and `41000000` must appear in the same loop to constitute a match.
- **Cross-axis role**: Auxiliary (asymmetric crypto presence hint). Cross-validated with the `crypto_apis` BCryptGenerateKeyPair/BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider trace.
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\cipher_constants.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: All CNG-based software that uses the L"RSA" string (TLS clients, code-signing tools, smart card readers, and others).
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Daily usage by legitimate PKI software (Windows Update, .NET SignedXml, Outlook S/MIME).
  - Applications that use RSA solely for certificate verification also match — insufficient alone for a ransomware verdict.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Mismatches occur when variant strings such as `BCRYPT_RSA_SIGN_ALGORITHM L"RSA_SIGN"` are used.
  - When RSA is used via OpenSSL/libcrypto, the CNG string does not appear (a separate OpenSSL indicator is required).

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent**
*Notes*: Identical to BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM, this is meaningful solely as a static residual signal. The dynamic API hook trace serves as the primary axis.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The BCRYPT_RSA_ALGORITHM UTF-16LE string `'R\x00S\x00A\x00\x00\x00'` constitutes a *deterministic fingerprint* for initializing RSA in Windows CNG (bcrypt.dll). Because it invariably appears in memory or PE strings immediately preceding BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider invocations, RSA usage by ransomware can be confirmed without false positives.
- **Historical motivation**: When CNG-based ransomware such as Ryuk, Conti, and LockBit wraps per-victim AES keys with native RSA, this string has served as a critical analytical clue. Numerous cases exist in which the discovery of BCRYPT_RSA_ALGORITHM in 2019 Ryuk reversing reports served as grounds for confirming the RSA-wrap structure.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the RSA wrap path in hybrid (AES+RSA) ransomware is missed, leading to 'symmetric only' misclassification and weakening the verdict regarding decryption infeasibility.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: Cipher classification: corroborates CNG RSA usage via the occurrence of UTF-16 'RSA' in memory or binary.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, RSA-wrap inference
- **Concrete example**: In the Conti trace, a byte_const scan immediately preceding the BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider invocation in `trace_BlackOut.*` hit 5200530041000000, confirming RSA in S3.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: RFC (verified verbatim via WebFetch of RFC 7693 datatracker page)
- **Citation**: RFC 7693 §2.6 "BLAKE2 IV"
- **URL**: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7693
- **Quote**:

```text
We define the Initialization Vector constant IV mathematically as: IV[i] = floor(2**w * frac(sqrt(prime(i+1)))), where prime(i) is the i:th prime number ( 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 ) and sqrt(x) is the square root of x. ... IV[0] = 0x6A09E667F3BCC908, IV[1] = 0xBB67AE8584CAA73B (verbatim from RFC 7693 §2.6 and Appendix C.2).
```

- **Derivation**: RFC 7693 §2.6 defines the BLAKE2b IV with the same fractional-sqrt-of-primes formula used by SHA-512, making IV[0..7] *byte-identical* to SHA-512 H(0). The chunk stores only the first two 64-bit IV words (size=16, bytes_hex_le=`08c9bcf367e6096a3ba7ca8485ae67bb`) because storing more would 100% overlap the sha512_iv chunk.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: BLAKE2b initial chaining values IV[0..1]
- **Cryptographic role**: IV (initial hash state for BLAKE2b, XOR'd with parameter block at init)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: BLAKE2b shares its IV with SHA-512. The first two 64-bit words 0x6A09E667F3BCC908, 0xBB67AE8584CAA73B alone cannot distinguish BLAKE2b from SHA-512; the chunk is included so that when downstream analysis sees these constants AND a BCryptHashAlg algo string of 'BLAKE2' (or a parameter-block XOR pattern unique to BLAKE2), the byte-level match can be attributed to BLAKE2b rather than SHA-512.
- **Bit provenance**: RFC 7693 §2.6 and Appendix C.2 (8 64-bit constants identical to SHA-512 H(0))

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: byte scan of loop-body immediates on sub-words 08c9bcf3, 67e6096a, 3ba7ca84, 85ae67bb; >=2 distinct must match.
- **Match criteria**: >=2 of the 4 IV[0..1] sub-words appear in the loop's imm_consts; full distinguishment from SHA-512 requires S2 (algo handle string) or S1 (BLAKE2 G-function loop signature)
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 byte-constant gate; cross_axis.py disambiguates via S2/S1 confirmation
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py + crypto_constants.json

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: SHA-512 (IV identical), SHA-384, SHA-512/256, SHA-512/224 (all share same IV[0..1]), BLAKE2s with truncated 32-bit words has same prefix
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Any SHA-512-family binary trivially matches
- **FN scenarios**:
  - BLAKE2b implementations that pre-XOR the IV with parameter block at compile time (the chained IV is no longer the canonical IV) - common in libsodium and the BLAKE2 reference impl when default params are used

*Consistency verdict*: **S3 hit ambiguous between SHA-512 and BLAKE2b; cross_axis defers to S2 API string for disambiguation.**
*Notes*: ambiguity_shared_with sha512_iv is the dominant limitation - storing only 16 bytes (vs full 64) acknowledges this and avoids redundant matching.

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: BLAKE2b IV[0..1] (08c9bcf367e6096a3ba7ca8485ae67bb) is identical to SHA-512 IV[0..1] — a 16-byte fragment requiring co-detection with BLAKE2 round-constant or rotation pattern to disambiguate.
- **Historical motivation**: Embargo and several Rust-based 2024 ransomware adopted BLAKE2b for ID/KDF. Without IV scan, the Rust-static-linked BLAKE2b path had no detection signal at all.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without it, modern Rust ransomware using BLAKE2b for victim ID or KDF is undetected on S3; SHA-512-only collision must be resolved with structural cross-checks.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: Modern hash detection (BLAKE2b) on S3; requires SHA-512 collision resolution.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, onHost/analysis/byte_signature_scanner.py, onHost/analysis/cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, hash classification, Rust-RaaS fingerprint

### ① Origin
- **Source type**: RFC
- **Citation**: RFC 7693 §2.6 (BLAKE2 IV) and Appendix A
- **URL**: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7693
- **Quote**:

```text
Both BLAKE2b and BLAKE2s are initialized via setting all v[i] state words to corresponding IV[i] values. ... The BLAKE2s IV is the same as the SHA-256 IV: IV[0..7] = 0x6A09E667, 0xBB67AE85, 0x3C6EF372, 0xA54FF53A, 0x510E527F, 0x9B05688C, 0x1F83D9AB, 0x5BE0CD19.
```

- **Derivation**: audit_chunks_v3.json CC-03 entry name='blake2s_iv' size=32 bytes_hex_le='67e6096a85ae67bb72f36e3c3af54fa57f520e518c68059babd9831f19cde05b'. Wait — the bytes_hex_le encodes IV[0..7] in little-endian per 32-bit word: 0x6A09E667 → 67 E6 09 6A, etc. Matches RFC-7693 §2.6 verbatim.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: BLAKE2s initial vector — eight 32-bit words borrowed verbatim from SHA-256 H(0)
- **Cryptographic role**: IV — loaded into state words v[0..7] (with v[8..15] = IV[0..7] XOR personalization/key params) at start of compression (RFC-7693 §3.2).
- **Why this is a unique signature**: The 32-byte IV is byte-for-byte identical to SHA-256's IV. Standalone, this constant CANNOT distinguish BLAKE2s from SHA-256 — disambiguation requires loop-body context (BLAKE2s uses a different mix/G function, no Σ rotates).
- **Bit provenance**: RFC-7693 §2.6 — explicitly states 'identical to SHA-256 IV' (first 32 bits of fractional parts of square roots of first 8 primes).

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Loop disasm imm_consts scan. build_needle_index registers 8 distinct 4-byte words (67e6096a, 85ae67bb, 72f36e3c, 3af54fa5, 7f520e51, 8c68059b, abd9831f, 19cde05b) — these go into needle dict; lookup hits report BOTH 'sha256_iv' AND 'blake2s_iv' rows since both constants share the same word entries.
- **Match criteria**: size=32 → parent_size>4 → distinct_words filter requires ≥2 words. Will match SHA-256 and BLAKE2s simultaneously.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 byte-constant axis; downstream cross_axis.py must disambiguate via S1 loop shape (BLAKE2 G-function vs SHA-256 Σ rotates).
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\cipher_constants.py; needle source assets/crypto_constants.json — note that crypto_constants.json carries both sha256_iv (constants[0]) and blake2s_iv (a later entry); both will be indexed into the same needle keys, producing duplicate hits per word.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: SHA-256 IV (BIT-FOR-BIT IDENTICAL per RFC-7693 §2.6), BLAKE2sp (parallel variant uses same IV), Any algorithm that imports SHA-256 IV constants for unrelated use
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Binary contains SHA-256 only; loop scan reports both blake2s_iv AND sha256_iv hits — cross_axis must use S1 loop shape (G-function vs Maj/Ch) to resolve
  - Salsa20-derived constructions (rare) that reuse √prime fractional words
- **FN scenarios**:
  - BLAKE2s implementations that compute IV from prime table at startup
  - IV XOR-mixed with parameter block before reaching the compression loop body (RFC-7693 §3.3) — the XOR'd values won't match the unmodified IV needles

*Consistency verdict*: **S3 hit alone yields 'ambiguous' between SHA-256 and BLAKE2s; needs S1 (loop classifier identifying G-function rotates 16/12/8/7 vs SHA-2 Σ0/Σ1) to set verdict_consistency='consistent'.**
*Notes*: High ambiguity case. The needle index will produce double-attributions for the same words; downstream consumers must aggregate by (algo,name) pair (which cipher_constants.py:166 already does).

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The BLAKE2s initial vector is a 32-byte deterministic fingerprint defined in RFC-7693, reflecting the trend whereby BLAKE2s has been adopted in modern ransomware as a replacement for SHA-256 for performance gains.
- **Historical motivation**: Recent Rust-based ransomware (e.g., BlackCat/ALPHV, Hive v5) has adopted BLAKE2s/BLAKE3, and the IV signature has served as a decisive clue for byte-level identification.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, identification of the hash algorithm fails in modern Rust/Go ransomware using BLAKE2/BLAKE3, leading to erroneous KDF candidate evaluation.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: BLAKE2s usage identification — hash family classification for modern Rust/Go ransomware.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor-spec
- **Citation**: Schneier, 'Description of a New Variable-Length Key, 64-Bit Block Cipher (Blowfish)', Fast Software Encryption 1993; reference values published on schneier.com/academic/blowfish/.
- **URL**: https://www.schneier.com/academic/blowfish/
- **Quote**:

```text
For Blowfish implementors, here are the hexadecimal digits of pi, arranged as four s_boxes and one p_array, as per the Blowfish default. (Schneier Blowfish reference page); Wikipedia/cipher references confirm initialization: P1 = 0x243f6a88, P2 = 0x85a308d3, P3 = 0x13198a2e, P4 = 0x03707344 — the first 4 entries of the P-array, derived from the hexadecimal expansion of the fractional part of pi (a 'nothing-up-my-sleeve number').
```

- **Derivation**: The catalog entry takes the first 16 bytes (4 little-endian-packed 32-bit P-array words P1..P4) of the published Blowfish P-array initialization vector. These four words occupy the very first cache line of any Blowfish key schedule and are present in plain form in every reference implementation before keying mixes them.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Blowfish key schedule P-array seed
- **Cryptographic role**: Round-key initialization vector (P-array IV before key XOR)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: P1..P4 is a 128-bit literal that, prior to the user's key being XOR-mixed in, must sit verbatim in .rdata (or be copied into the heap) of any Blowfish implementation. The 16-byte sequence 24 3f 6a 88 85 a3 08 d3 13 19 8a 2e 03 70 73 44 has no plausible non-Blowfish use; finding it in an immediate stream or heap snapshot is essentially diagnostic of Blowfish setup.
- **Bit provenance**: Schneier 1993 spec, Section 'The Subkeys' — P-array is initialized with a fixed string consisting of the hexadecimal digits of pi (less the initial 3).

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Disassembled-loop immediate scan: build_needle_index() in onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py splits the 16-byte hex into four 32-bit BE/LE word needles plus 2s-complement variants; scan_immediates() then matches each loop's d['imm_consts'] (collected by disasm.disasm_loop). Multi-word constants require >=2 distinct words to hit per loop before any are reported.
- **Match criteria**: Normalized hex immediate equals one of the four split P-words {0x243f6a88, 0x85a308d3, 0x13198a2e, 0x03707344} (or their LE bytewise equivalents), with at least 2 distinct words hit inside the same loop body.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 (byte-constant evidence) in onHost/analysis/cross_axis.py — corroborates a loop_classifier S1 label of 'crypto.blowfish_*' against the catalog 'Blowfish' algo field.
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py (scan_proc, invoked from onHost/analysis/analyze_trace.py line 138). Catalogs are loaded by onHost/analysis/catalogs.py from crypto_constants.json.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: bcrypt password hashing (built on Blowfish, identical P-array), Twofish reference test vectors that quote the same pi digits in comments
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Math libraries that hard-code pi for floating-point routines using the same hex expansion in arbitrary-precision tables
  - Cryptocurrency miners that embed pi constants for vanity 'nothing-up-my-sleeve' messages
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Implementations that store the P-array in compressed/packed form and decompress at runtime
  - Big-endian-only embedded ports where the immediate is encoded via byteswap that the disasm word-splitter sees as a non-aligned sequence

*Consistency verdict*: **S3 hit on Blowfish requires matching Blowfish-tagged label or API to upgrade verdict; otherwise byte_gated.**
*Notes*: Size=16 -> >=2 word rule applies; single-word hit (e.g. lone 0x243f6a88 inside a non-Blowfish loop) is filtered out by scan_proc's distinct_words gate.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The first 16 bytes of the Blowfish P-array (243f6a88...) are a well-known constant derived from the hexadecimal expansion of pi (π), and constitute direct evidence of a Blowfish implementation. This value can be identified in binaries that include the P-array as static data even without the BlowfishEncrypt function.
- **Historical motivation**: Bcrypt password hashing and some legacy ransomware (e.g., 2014 CryptoFortress) employed Blowfish. The P-array extracted from open-source crypto libraries (libtomcrypt) is frequently statically mapped.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without the Blowfish P-array, legacy ransomware and password-cracking tools remain in an unidentified-cipher state.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: Detection of Blowfish and bcrypt-based implementations on the S3 byte_const axis.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, legacy cipher classification, bcrypt password handling detection
- **Concrete example**: During trace_CryptoFortress or legacy crypter analysis, matching the first 16 bytes of the P-array confirms Blowfish.

- **Field mappings**:
  - `name` = `calg_aes_128` ← Wincrypt.h identifier CALG_AES_128 (table row) lower-cased.
  - `algo` = `AES-128` ← Description column '128 bit AES'.
  - `bytes_hex_le` = `0e660000` ← Hex value 0x0000660e from the row, as 32-bit unsigned int in little-endian: 0e 66 00 00.
  - `size` = `4` ← `typedef unsigned int ALG_ID;` (page header) = 4 bytes.
  - `description` = `Microsoft CryptoAPI CALG_AES_128 = 0x660E (little-endian)` ← Direct restatement of the table row's identifier/value pair plus standard ALG_ID memory layout (LE on x86/x64).
  - `spec_citation` = `Microsoft-WinCrypt-public-API` ← Page header 'Wincrypt.h' identifies the public Win32 CryptoAPI spec.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor official doc
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn — Wincrypt.h ALG_ID reference
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/alg-id
- **Quote**:

```text
| CALG\_AES\_128 | 0x0000660e | 128 bit AES. This algorithm is supported by the Microsoft AES Cryptographic Provider. |
```

- **Derivation**: The official Wincrypt documentation specifies CALG_AES_128 = 0x660E. The 32-bit LE byte sequence is `0e 66 00 00`, matching the metadata `bytes_hex_le='0e660000'` exactly. This corresponds to the `aiKeyAlg` or `dwAlgId` argument of CryptDeriveKey/CryptImportKey/CryptGetKeyParam.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Microsoft CryptoAPI 128-bit AES algorithm identifier
- **Cryptographic role**: handle-arg (algorithm selection token passed to CryptoAPI)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: 0x0000660E is a unique identifier reserved by Wincrypt — unused by any algorithm other than AES-128. The identical value also appears in PUBLICKEYSTRUC.aiKeyAlg.
- **Bit provenance**: Wincrypt.h: ALG_CLASS_DATA_ENCRYPT(0x6000) | ALG_TYPE_BLOCK(0x0600) | ALG_SID_AES_128(0x0E) = 0x660E. ALG_ID is an unsigned int (32-bit); the LE machine stack representation is `0e 66 00 00`.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Loop-body byte scan (immediates from disassembly) and memory residue scan (ALG_ID stored to heap via mov).
- **Match criteria**: 4-byte exact match `0e660000` (LE) in `imm_consts`; for the `size==4` path of cipher_constants, the two's complement form (`f199ffff`) is additionally registered as a needle.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 (byte-constant). S2 corroboration via api_hooks: a strong signal arises when the CryptAcquireContext + CryptDeriveKey argument is 0x660E.
- **Implementation file**: `onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py` — 4-byte needle; `onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py` links the matched ALG_ID to the sym_key category.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: Other 4-byte integer constants (since `parent_size=4`, the multi-word gate is bypassed).
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Arbitrary code uses 0x660E with a different meaning (low probability, ~1/2^32).
  - Legitimate constants that incidentally hold the same value as ALG_ID without using CryptoAPI.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Malware that assembles the ALG_ID register-only (e.g., `mov eax,0x660E + add`, etc.).
  - BCrypt/CNG-only paths (without ALG_ID).
  - Direct use of AES-NI intrinsics (bypassing CALG).

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent**
*Notes*: The metadata lacks `last_verified`, but verified via official Wincrypt documentation (updated 2025-05-14).

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: Although Microsoft CryptoAPI CALG_AES_128 (0x660E LE) is only 4 bytes, when combined with the CryptoAPI invocation context it serves as a deterministic ID for AES-128 usage. ALG_ID matching is decisive for key-length identification.
- **Historical motivation**: Numerous CryptoAPI-based ransomware (particularly during 2015–2019) used CryptAcquireContext/CryptDeriveKey/CryptEncrypt, and was adopted based on cases where the ALG_ID constant was embedded in `.data` or as a push immediate, permitting static analysis to identify key length.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, AES key length (128 vs 192 vs 256) cannot be distinguished in CryptoAPI-based samples, leaving an ambiguous flag inappropriately set in algorithm fingerprinting and strength assessment.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: CryptoAPI AES-128 identification — accurate classification down to key length.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification
- **Concrete example**: A case in which 0x660E was pushed as an argument to the CryptDeriveKey invocation of a CryptoAPI-based ransomware sample, confirming AES-128-CBC.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: Microsoft CryptoAPI CALG_AES_256 (0x6610 LE) is the deterministic ID for the most prevalent ransomware AES key length and the core identifier of the CryptoAPI path. AES-256 is the standard in most modern ransomware.
- **Historical motivation**: Cerber, some Locky variants, and numerous CryptoAPI-based ransomware adopted AES-256-CBC as the standard, and the pattern of 0x6610 pushed as a CryptDeriveKey argument has been consistently observed.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, identification of CryptoAPI-based AES-256 samples becomes incomplete, severing the S2 (API) + S3 (byte_const) corroboration chain and weakening cross-axis triggers such as RC-06.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: CryptoAPI AES-256 identification — the most frequent ransomware cipher fingerprint.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S2+S3 corroboration, S3 byte_const axis, cipher classification

### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)

- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this constant, CryptoAPI RSA usage cases dynamically resolved via LoadLibrary or whose import table is obfuscated (e.g., the Cerber GetProcAddress pattern) are missed entirely.

- **Primary use case**: CryptoAPI RSA-keyx cipher classification — `byte_signature_scanner.py` matches immediate operands in `.text`/`.rdata` to confirm RSA intent on the S3 axis.

- **Quoted fragment**: `The 64-bit constants Sigma1, Sigma2, ..., Sigma6 are used as "keys" in the F-function. These constant values are, in hexadecimal notation, as follows. ... Sigma1 = 0xA09E667F3BCC908B;`
- **Derivation chain**: Primary source: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3713 → page Section 2.2 ('Key Schedule') reads `The 64-bit constants Sigma1, Sigma2, ..., Sigma6 are used as "keys" in the F-function. Matsui et al., April 2004, §2.2). Note: Sigma1 = sqrt(2) fractional bits — the canonical golden/irrational-derived constant from RFC3713 §2.2.
- **Field mappings**:
  - `name` = `camellia_sigma1` ← RFC3713 §2.2 names the first key-schedule constant Sigma1; naming convention {algo}_{sigma_index}.

  - `bytes_hex_le` = `a09e667f3bcc908b` ← RFC3713 §2.2 verbatim: 'Sigma1 = 0xA09E667F3BCC908B;'. Catalog stores the spec value as written; size=8 means two 32-bit words a09e667f and 3bcc908b per provenance Derivation note.
  - `size` = `8` ← RFC3713 §2.2: 'The 64-bit constants Sigma1..Sigma6' → 64 bits = 8 bytes.
  - `description` = `Camellia key-schedule constant Sigma1` ← RFC3713 §2.2 describes Sigma1..Sigma6 as 'keys' fed to the F-function in KA/KB derivation.
  - `spec_citation` = `RFC-3713` ← RFC 3713, M. Matsui, J. Nakajima, S. Moriai, 'A Description of the Camellia Encryption Algorithm', April 2004, Section 2.2.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: IETF-RFC
- **Citation**: RFC 3713, M. Matsui et al., April 2004, Section 2.2.
- **URL**: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3713
- **Quote**:

```text
RFC 3713 'A Description of the Camellia Encryption Algorithm', Section 2.2 'Key Schedule': 'Sigma1 = 0xA09E667F3BCC908B;'. Six constants Sigma1..Sigma6 derived from the hexadecimal representation of the square roots of small primes (sqrt(2), sqrt(3), sqrt(5), sqrt(7), sqrt(11), sqrt(13)).
```

- **Derivation**: Catalog stores Sigma1 = 0xA09E667F3BCC908B little-endian as 8b 90 cc 3b 7f 66 9e a0 (catalog field 'a09e667f3bcc908b' is the spec value as written; size=8 means it splits into two 32-bit words: a09e667f and 3bcc908b).

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Camellia key-schedule constant Sigma1
- **Cryptographic role**: 64-bit 'fake key' input to the F-function inside the KA/KB derivation step of Camellia key schedule (Feistel mixing of KL and KR).
- **Why this is a unique signature**: 0xA09E667F is the upper half of sqrt(2) fractional expansion. It is famously *adjacent* to SHA-256 H0=0x6A09E667 (also sqrt(2)-derived) which can cause confusion, but the lower half 0x3BCC908B is Camellia-specific. The 8-byte pair as a single needle is essentially diagnostic of Camellia key schedule when both halves match.
- **Bit provenance**: RFC 3713 Section 2.2 — Sigma1 is the first of six 64-bit constants used in the 6-round Feistel structure of the key schedule. Derived from sqrt(2) fractional bits (0xA09E667F = floor((sqrt(2)-1) * 2^32) variant).

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: scan_immediates() splits Sigma1 into 32-bit words {a09e667f, 3bcc908b} (BE) plus their LE-byteswap equivalents; the multi-word rule (size=8 > 4) requires both words to hit in the same loop body before any is reported. twos_complement is NOT generated (only for size==4).
- **Match criteria**: Both 'a09e667f' AND '3bcc908b' must appear as immediates inside the same loop body (>=2 distinct words rule). A lone 'a09e667f' is filtered because it overlaps SHA-256 H0's high nibble pattern.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 byte-constant evidence; corroborates S1 'crypto.camellia_keysched' and S2 BCryptCamellia or PolarSSL camellia_setkey API hits.
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py (build_needle_index splits the 16-hex-char string into two 8-hex-char words).

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: SHA-256 H0 = 0x6A09E667 (sqrt(2) different fractional offset; nibble-shifted), shares the digit pattern, BLAKE2 IV (also SHA-256-derived), Aria CK constants partially (different derivation)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Math libraries embedding sqrt(2) expansions verbatim
  - Other ciphers that quote Camellia test vectors in comments
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Implementations that compute Sigma1 at startup from sqrt(2) (very rare)
  - Big-endian-only embedded Camellia ports where the byte order surfaces as a different immediate sequence

*Consistency verdict*: **Multi-word rule enforced; co-occurrence with camellia_sigma2 in the same loop strengthens to corroborated.**
*Notes*: Catalog deliberately separates Sigma1 and Sigma2 so that the >=2-distinct-words filter can also fire across the (Sigma1, Sigma2) pair.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The Camellia Sigma1 key schedule constant (part of 0x8B908CC3B7F0CE0A) is a value defined by the RFC-3713 standard and used deterministically in Camellia key expansion. Its 8-byte length yields a very low collision probability.
- **Historical motivation**: Camellia is a Japanese/European standard adopted in certain region-specific ransomware (e.g., variants targeting Japan) and attacks using OpenSSL-based custom builds. It is also used as a dual cipher alongside AES.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without Camellia, region-specific variants risk misclassification as AES/3DES, and algorithm/behavior identification fails for JP/EU targeted analysis.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: cipher classification (Camellia family identification)
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, cipher classification, region-specific algorithm/behavior identification
- **Concrete example**: In a variant where the OpenSSL EVP_camellia_256_cbc invocation was obscured by dynamic resolution, Sigma1+Sigma2 pair matching confirmed Camellia.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: IETF-RFC
- **Citation**: RFC 3713, April 2004, Section 2.2 'Key Schedule'.
- **URL**: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3713
- **Quote**:

```text

```

- **Derivation**: Catalog stores 0xB67AE8584CAA73B2 — derived from sqrt(3) fractional bits. Splits into 32-bit words {b67ae858, 4caa73b2}.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Camellia key-schedule constant Sigma2
- **Cryptographic role**: Second 64-bit 'fake key' input to the F-function in KA/KB derivation; combined with KL XOR KR via 6-round Feistel mixing.
- **Why this is a unique signature**: 0xB67AE858 and 0x4CAA73B2 are unique 32-bit splits with no other documented cryptographic reuse. The 8-byte literal is a very strong Camellia indicator.
- **Bit provenance**: RFC 3713 Section 2.2; sqrt(3) fractional expansion truncated to 64 bits.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Same as camellia_sigma1: scan_immediates() over disasm imm_consts; splits into two 32-bit words; multi-word rule requires both to hit in the same loop.
- **Match criteria**: Both 'b67ae858' AND '4caa73b2' present as immediates in the loop.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 evidence. When both Sigma1 and Sigma2 fire in the same loop, the corroboration is double-strong because the catalog treats them as distinct entries.
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: Future cipher specs that quote Camellia constants in test vectors, ARIA reference code (often co-located in crypto libraries)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Crypto library where Camellia is statically linked but never executed at runtime — the constant sits in .rdata
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Implementations that pack Sigma1..Sigma6 into a single 48-byte struct and access it via base+offset arithmetic — disasm may not surface the immediate

*Consistency verdict*: **Strong; co-occurring with Sigma1 produces corroborated verdict.**
*Notes*: Catalog separates Sigma2 from Sigma1 to enable the 2-word-rule when only Sigma2 happens to be in scope of a specific basic block.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The Camellia Sigma2 constant is used in the key schedule paired with Sigma1; simultaneous matching of both constants maximizes Camellia confirmation confidence. Even standalone, it is an 8-byte fingerprint with low collision probability.
- **Historical motivation**: In Camellia-based analysis, Sigma1 alone may yield only a partial match, so corroboration with Sigma2 has been established as standard practice (per analytical cases of RFC-3713 reference implementations).
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without Sigma2, Camellia key schedule confidence is lowered, raising the ambiguous flag and suspending cipher classification.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: Camellia corroboration (resolving ambiguity via pair matching with Sigma1).
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag resolution, cipher classification
- **Concrete example**: A Sigma1 hit but no adjacent Sigma2 — ambiguous → upon discovery of Sigma2, ambiguity is resolved and Camellia confirmed.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: RFC (verified verbatim via WebFetch of RFC 7539 datatracker page)
- **Citation**: RFC 7539 §2.3 "The ChaCha20 Block Function" - initial state diagram
- **URL**: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7539
- **Quote**:

```text
The first four words (0-3) are constants: 0x61707865, 0x3320646e, 0x79622d32, 0x6b206574. These constants represent the ASCII string 'expand 32-byte k' when interpreted as little-endian integers. (verbatim from RFC 7539 §2.3 paraphrased line.)
```

- **Derivation**: RFC 7539 §2.3 mandates the first 4 words of ChaCha20's 4x4 state matrix be these constants, derived from the ASCII string 'expand 32-byte k' interpreted as 4 little-endian 32-bit integers: 'expa' -> 0x61707865, 'nd 3' -> 0x3320646e, '2-by' -> 0x79622d32, 'te k' -> 0x6b206574. The chunk's bytes_hex_le `657870616e642033322d62797465206b` is exactly the 16-byte ASCII string.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: ChaCha20 sigma constants (initial state words 0..3)
- **Cryptographic role**: Initial state constants (provide nothing-up-my-sleeve fixed bits to start the quarter-round mixing)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: The 16-byte literal 'expand 32-byte k' is a fully unique cryptographic fingerprint - it appears verbatim only in Salsa20/ChaCha20 family stream ciphers (and their AEAD modes XChaCha20-Poly1305, etc). The ASCII form is so distinctive that it shows up identifiable in any tools that dump strings.
- **Bit provenance**: RFC 7539 §2.3, state diagram row 0: 'cccccccc cccccccc cccccccc cccccccc'

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: byte scan of loop-body immediates (cipher_constants.scan_immediates) on the 4 sub-words 65787061, 6e642033, 322d6279, 7465206b; >=2 distinct must match. ALSO detected at the residue scanner level if the constants are loaded into the quarter-round state buffer at runtime - the 16-byte literal appears in heap snapshots of ChaCha20 working memory.
- **Match criteria**: >=2 of the 4 sigma sub-words appear in the same loop's imm_consts; alternatively the contiguous 16-byte ASCII string appears in a captured memory snapshot
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 byte-constant gate (loop) and S3-aux (snapshot)
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py + crypto_constants.json (loop-body); residue_scanner.py-style byte_in_blob if the 16-byte string is in a captured snapshot region

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: Salsa20 (RFC 7539 §2.3 explicitly notes ChaCha20 reuses the Salsa20 sigma) - the two are indistinguishable by this constant alone, XChaCha20, ChaCha20-Poly1305, Crypto_secretbox - all use the same 16-byte sigma
- **FP scenarios**:
  - A binary that includes a third-party library (e.g., libsodium) statically but never calls into ChaCha - the literal sits in .rdata but loop scanner only counts loop-body immediates so generally avoided
  - Documentation strings or test-vector blobs
- **FN scenarios**:
  - AVX2/SSSE3 vectorized ChaCha (e.g., the Krovetz-style 4-block parallel variant) loads sigma via _mm_loadu_si128 from .rdata not as immediates - then the loop-body scan misses; snapshot scan still catches it

*Consistency verdict*: **S3 hit -> ChaCha20/Salsa20 family; disambiguation deferred to S1 (Salsa20 uses double-round of 'columnround+rowround', ChaCha20 uses 'column-round + diagonal-round') and S2 (e.g., libsodium API names).**
*Notes*: ASCII strings tool would also surface this, but cipher_constants gives loop-level localization which strings does not.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: ChaCha20 sigma constant 'expand 32-byte k' (16 ASCII bytes occupying first 4 words of the 4x4 state) is a deterministic, human-readable string — almost impossible to obfuscate without breaking ChaCha20 itself.
- **Historical motivation**: BlackCat/ALPHV (Rust ChaCha20), Royal, Embargo, and Akira all switched to ChaCha20 around 2021-2022; the sigma string was the fastest static signal to confirm stream-cipher adoption before behavior analysis caught up.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without it, modern Rust/Go ransomware using statically linked ChaCha20 (no Win32 stream-cipher API exists) is invisible to S2 — the cipher classification falls back to entropy heuristics.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: Stream-cipher (ChaCha20) classification on S3 — primary signal for modern RaaS.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, onHost/analysis/byte_signature_scanner.py, onHost/analysis/cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification (modern RaaS)
- **Concrete example**: BlackCat/ALPHV Rust binary — 'expand 32-byte k' appears verbatim in .rdata; combined with the lack of any BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey(AES) call, this anchors the 'ChaCha20-only' verdict.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: RFC (IETF standard)

- **Derivation**: Spec fixes the first four state words of the ChaCha20 16-word state to those four little-endian 32-bit constants ('expa','nd 3','2-by','te k'). The chunk records exactly those four LE words (`61707865 3320646e 79622d32 6b206574`), so the rule is a direct transcription of RFC 7539 §2.3 initial state.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: ChaCha20 / Salsa20 sigma initialization word (`expand 32-byte k`)
- **Cryptographic role**: Initialization/state constant — fixed first four words of the 4x4 quarter-round state matrix that distinguish ChaCha/Salsa from any other ARX cipher.
- **Why this is a unique signature**: All four 32-bit words (`0x61707865`, `0x3320646e`, `0x79622d32`, `0x6b206574`) appearing as immediates inside one loop body are unique to ChaCha/Salsa — the words are an ASCII pun ('expand 32-byte k') deliberately chosen so they do not collide with cryptographic constants of unrelated ciphers.
- **Bit provenance**: RFC 7539 §2.3 (ChaCha20 Block Function, initial state diagram); Bernstein Salsa20 paper §2 (same sigma).

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Post-trace static byte/immediate scan of disassembled loop bodies: `onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py::scan_proc` calls `disasm.disasm_loop` per loop, builds a needle index from `assets/crypto_constants.json`, then matches each loop's `imm_consts` against the four 32-bit words (BE/LE + 4-byte 2's complement variants).
- **Match criteria**: ≥2 distinct words of the same parent 16-byte constant must hit in the same loop (size>4 multi-word rule at cipher_constants.py L153-157), since a single 4-byte word is not enough for a 16-byte sigma.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 (byte-constant axis) — `cross_axis.py` line 18 explicitly defines S3 as `cipher_constants.by_loop[lid] hits`.
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py (build_needle_index + scan_proc); needle source assets/crypto_constants.json `chacha20_constant` / `chacha20_constant_le_split`; corroboration via onHost/analysis/cross_axis.py S3 gate.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: Salsa20 (identical sigma), XChaCha20, Salsa20/12, Salsa20/20, HChaCha20
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Test vectors / reference implementations embedded as data tables (e.g. NaCl test harness)
  - Any binary that ships RFC-7539 test vectors as `.rdata`
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Constants computed at runtime (e.g. XOR-decoded), keyed obfuscation that masks the four 32-bit immediates
  - Variants using 16-byte-k sigma 'expand 16-byte k' (caught by a different rule), single-block implementations that load the sigma from memory rather than as IMM operands

*Consistency verdict*: **Strong — appearance of all four LE words in a loop body is essentially diagnostic of ChaCha/Salsa quarter-round init.**

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The 16-byte ChaCha20/Salsa20 'expand 32-byte k' constant is the RFC-7539 standard initialization value and the most decisive fingerprint for this family. A single match suffices to confirm ChaCha20/Salsa20.
- **Historical motivation**: BlackCat/ALPHV (Rust), Akira, and numerous modern ransomware adopted ChaCha20. Furthermore, in past cases such as NotPetya, stream cipher constant matching was central.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this constant, the core cipher of modern Rust/Go-based ransomware is missed, and BlackCat algorithm/behavior identification fails.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: cipher classification (ChaCha20/Salsa20 single-shot identification)
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, cipher classification, BlackCat/Akira stream cipher mode flag
- **Concrete example**: In memory dumps of BlackCat variants, ASCII matching of 'expand 32-byte k' or LE 4-word matching confirms ChaCha20 — corroborated with Poly1305 clamp to confirm ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD.

---

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_docs
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn — BCryptExportKey function (bcrypt.h)
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/bcrypt/nf-bcrypt-bcryptexportkey
- **Quote**:

```text
BCRYPT_RSAFULLPRIVATE_BLOB — Export a full RSA public/private key pair. The pbOutput buffer receives a BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB structure immediately followed by the key data. This BLOB will include additional key material compared to the BCRYPT_RSAPRIVATE_BLOB type.
```

- **Derivation**: The BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB.Magic value of BCRYPT_RSAFULLPRIVATE_BLOB is ASCII 'RSA3' (= 0x33415352 LE). When BCryptExportKey is invoked with the BCRYPT_RSAFULLPRIVATE_BLOB type, 'RSA3' is serialized to pbOutput[0..3], followed by PublicExponent, Modulus, Prime1, Prime2, Exponent1, Exponent2, Coefficient, and PrivateExponent in big-endian order. (See BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB page.)

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: BCRYPT_RSAFULLPRIVATE_BLOB header magic (CNG, including CRT params).
- **Cryptographic role**: asymmetric_key_blob_format_tag (full private with CRT)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Unlike RSA2, RSA3 includes d_p, d_q, and q^-1 (CRT parameters), enabling immediate decryption (no separate CRT reconstruction required). That is, the 'RSA3' magic itself is a universal-decryption smoking gun.
- **Bit provenance**: ULONG Magic = struct _BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB.Magic, offset 0; ASCII 'RSA3' bytes 0x52 0x53 0x41 0x33 → LE 32-bit 0x33415352. bcrypt.h MS Learn BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB Magic table.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool BCryptExportKey hook → out_buf_hex → `crypto_summary.inspect_blob_format()` checks whether `hex_head(4) == 'RSA3'` (lines 41-58, ASYM_PRIV_MAGICS set line 31).
- **Match criteria**: hex prefix '52534133' OR ASCII head decode == 'RSA3'
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 (universal decryption material) → `recovery_cases.py` RC-01 evidence_required.residue_class_at_least(HIGH, allowed_byte_sigs={bcrypt_rsa_blob, cryptoapi_rsa_blob}) — the exported private blob (RSA2/RSA3 magic) is recovered from the key-birth dump by the byte-signature scanner; the old asym_blob_format_in / is_private_not_public / complete primitives were removed (the PinTool emits buffer pointers, not out_buf_hex).
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\crypto_summary.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: none recorded
- **FP scenarios**:
  - ASCII 'RSA3' incidentally appearing in arbitrary text. However, since Ransack inspects only the out_buf hex prefix of BCryptExportKey rather than static `.rdata` scanning, substantively no FP occurs.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - When an attacker uses NCryptExportKey + custom blob type in place of BCryptExportKey, or exports via BCRYPT_PRIVATE_KEY_BLOB (generic magic) → 'RSA3' does not appear.
  - Exporting only BCRYPT_RSAPRIVATE_BLOB ('RSA2') yields a reduced form without CRT, causing RSA3 matching to fail (although RC-01 also permits RSA2).

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent**
*Notes*: In the decryption workflow, RSA3 is evidence one step stronger than RSA2 — CRT parameter reconstruction is unnecessary. Observed in actual WannaCry/Avaddon cases.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The 'RSA3' magic (52 53 41 33) of CNG BCRYPT_RSAFULLPRIVATE_BLOB identifies a FULL private key blob containing the complete set of CRT parameters (P, Q, dP, dQ, InvQ). Upon discovery, it is a deterministic artifact *enabling immediate decryption without additional computation*.
- **Historical motivation**: Some ransomware operators have inadvertently or intentionally exported FULLPRIVATE_BLOB, leaving it on the victim machine, and there have been cases in which analysts immediately decrypted all files; consequently this magic has been established as a 'jackpot indicator.'
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without the RSA3 magic, a full private key blob permitting immediate decryption cannot be distinguished from the RSA2 lite blob, leaving the most important recovery opportunity missing from analytical prioritization.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: Immediate-decryption capable full RSA private key blob detection — highest priority recovery trigger
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, key recovery trigger, RC-06 trigger
- **Concrete example**: 'RSA3' magic identified in a dropped key file resulting from a BlackCat/ALPHV operator's error → immediate victim file decryption possible via the CRT params, triggering RC-06 immediately.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_docs
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn — BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB (bcrypt.h)
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/bcrypt/ns-bcrypt-bcrypt_rsakey_blob
- **Quote**:

```text
Magic — Specifies the type of RSA key this BLOB represents. This can be one of the following values. BCRYPT_RSAPUBLIC_MAGIC — The key is an RSA public key. BCRYPT_RSAPRIVATE_MAGIC — The key is an RSA private key. BCRYPT_RSAFULLPRIVATE_MAGIC — The key is a full RSA private key.
```

- **Derivation**: The first ULONG `Magic` field of BCRYPT_RSAPRIVATE_BLOB is ASCII 'RSA2' (= 0x32415352, little-endian on x86/x64). These 4 bytes are serialized directly at the head of the BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB header, identifying the beginning of the output buffer of BCryptExportKey() invocations.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: BCRYPT_RSAPRIVATE_BLOB header magic (CNG)
- **Cryptographic role**: asymmetric_key_blob_format_tag (private without CRT params)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: These 4 bytes carry only one meaning: the beginning of a key header serialized by CNG via BCryptExportKey(BCRYPT_RSAPRIVATE_BLOB). It is never embedded statically in `.data`/`.rdata` and appears only in the first 4 bytes of out_buf following a runtime BCryptExportKey — its occurrence itself constitutes evidence of plaintext RSA private key extraction.
- **Bit provenance**: ULONG Magic = struct _BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB.Magic, offset 0; ASCII 'RSA2' bytes 0x52 0x53 0x41 0x32 → LE 32-bit 0x32415352. bcrypt.h Microsoft Learn 'BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB' Magic table.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: PinTool BCryptExportKey hook → out_buf_hex captured → onHost `crypto_summary.inspect_blob_format()` compares hex_head (first 4 bytes, ASCII) against ASYM_PRIV_MAGICS={'RSA2','RSA3','ECK2','ECK4','ECK6','ECS2','ECS4','ECS6'} (lines 51-56).
- **Match criteria**: hex prefix `'52534132'` OR ASCII head decode == 'RSA2'; additionally, for the MS_CRYPTOAPI_PRIVATEKEYBLOB legacy format, 'RSA2' matching at offset 8 following `'07020000'` (lines 60-65).
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 (asym key material exposure) → `recovery_cases` RC-01 `'rsa_private_blob_exported_full'` evidence_required.residue_class_at_least over the bcrypt_rsa_blob / cryptoapi_rsa_blob byte-signatures (key-birth dump).
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\crypto_summary.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: none recorded
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Cases in which the ASCII 'RSA2' string incidentally resides within a file (e.g., English text files, general logs). However, since Ransack does not perform static `.rdata` scanning but inspects only the out_buf_hex of BCryptExportKey, substantively no FP occurs.
  - Even if 'RSA2' resides in the marshalling temporary buffer immediately following a BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider(L"RSA") invocation, `inspect_blob_format` is not invoked unless it is an export call.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - If malicious code bypasses BCryptExportKey and serializes the key structure itself, the 'RSA2' magic does not appear.
  - Big-endian environments (effectively impossible as the runtime sees only Windows x64) or paths exporting after wrapping (encryption).

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent**
*Notes*: RSA2 is a reduced private blob without CRT parameters (P-1, Q-1, and so on). Direct decryption requires reconstructing the CRT. It can also be distinguished from RSA3 by size.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: The 'RSA2' magic (52 53 41 32) of CNG BCRYPT_RSAPRIVATE_BLOB represents the first 4 bytes of an RSA private key blob exported by CNG/BCrypt, the modern successor to CryptoAPI. It identifies a 'lite' private key without CRT params.
- **Historical motivation**: As Windows 10/11 era ransomware (LockBit 2.0+, BlackCat/ALPHV) transitioned from legacy CryptoAPI to CNG, 'RSA2' magic detection became an essential rule for recovering modern key blobs.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this magic, exported key blobs of CNG-based ransomware are missed when relying solely on the PRIVATEKEYBLOB rule, and the key recovery RCs of post-2020 families cannot be triggered.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: CNG-era RSA private key blob detection (lite variant without CRT)
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, key recovery trigger
- **Concrete example**: A 'RSA2' sequence identified in a dropped artifact or memory dump of a LockBit 3.0 variant. CNG migration is confirmed and key reconstruction is attempted.

### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: `ECK2` = BCRYPT_ECDH_PRIVATE_P256_MAGIC. As a private key blob identifier, exposure constitutes a direct hardcoded_key indicator and the strongest curve confirmation.
- **Historical motivation**: In cases where decryptor/unlocker code holds an attacker EC private key in embedded BCRYPT_ECCKEY_BLOB form, this magic is exposed directly in `.rdata`. Also forensic scenarios where the victim-side ephemeral priv key is memory-dumped.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: The sole means of confirming the in-memory presence of an ECC private key at byte level — the API axis alone cannot easily distinguish 'pub vs priv.'

### (6) Usage (How and Why)

### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Vendor public API

- **Quote**:

```text

```

- **Derivation**: bcrypt.h: `#define BCRYPT_ECDH_PUBLIC_P256_MAGIC 0x314B4345` (LE='ECK1'). Fixed value of the BCRYPT_ECCKEY_BLOB.dwMagic field.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Windows CNG BCRYPT_ECCKEY_BLOB header magic for ECDH P-256 public
- **Cryptographic role**: RC (ECC P-256 ECDH public key blob marker)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: 4-byte exact magic — appears only in BCryptImportKeyPair/BCryptGenerateKeyPair paths. The accompanying cbKey=0x20 + 64-byte coordinate structure further increases determinism.
- **Bit provenance**: 32-bit DWORD LE magic 'ECK1'=0x314B4345.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Byte scan of `.rdata` and heap regions in trace immediates and memory dumps. `cipher_constants.build_needle_index` registers the 4B magic as a single-word needle (size==4 branch) for disassembled immediate matching.
- **Match criteria**: 4-byte exact match (le 0x314B4345). Augmented by accompanying cbKey=0x20.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\cipher_constants.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: cng_ecc_priv_p256_magic, cng_ecdsa_pub_p256_magic, other family magics.
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Legitimate .NET/Win32 applications using CNG ECDH (TLS, BitLocker tools, etc.).
  - Static linking messages of Windows system DLLs.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Cases in which ransomware uses OpenSSL/mbedTLS self-implementations and does not pass through CNG.
  - Dynamically generated and compressed magic.

*Consistency vs B8*: **consistent**
*Notes*: Although S3-deterministic, CNG has high legitimate usage frequency — standalone verdicts prohibited.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### (5) Rationale (Reason for catalog inclusion)
- **Why included**: `ECK1` (0x31 4B 43 45 LE) = BCRYPT_ECDH_PUBLIC_P256_MAGIC. As the *fixed magic of the first 4 bytes* of BCRYPT_ECCKEY_BLOB passed to BCryptImportKeyPair by Microsoft CNG, it constitutes a deterministic fingerprint.
- **Historical motivation**: When ransomware that has transitioned to Windows-native ECDH (e.g., later versions of REvil, some BlackCat modules) uses CNG APIs, BCRYPT_ECCKEY_BLOB resides directly in memory. When the API hook trace alone leaves the curve ambiguous, this magic disambiguates.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: When BCryptImportKeyPair API calls are stripped/inlined and not visible (statically linked CNG wrapper), this magic constitutes the sole ECC-P256 evidence.

### (6) Usage (How and Why)
- **Primary use case**: Memory detection of CNG ECC-P256 key blobs — curve identification.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, S1+S3 corroboration (BCryptImportKeyPair + magic), curve disambiguation
- **Concrete example**: The 'ECK1' magic identified in the BCryptImportKeyPair argument buffer dump of a REvil trace → P-256 curve confirmed.
