- **Derivation chain**: Primary source: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1321 (RFC 1321 — The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm, §3.4 Step 4 + Appendix A.3 md5c.c reference implementation) → page line 748 (EXACT_SUBSTRING citation in line_citations) reads `a = b + ((a + F(b,c,d) + X[k] + T[i]) <<< s). */` — the round-1 operation definition; and the immediately following Round 1 block in Appendix A.3 (md5c.c, around lines 309-324 per WebFetch of rfc1321.txt) reads `/* Round 1 */ FF (a, b, c, d, x[ 0], S11, 0xd76aa478); /* 1 */ FF (d, a, b, c, x[ 1], S12, 0xe8c7b756); /* 2 */ FF (c, d, a, b, x[ 2], S13, 0x242070db); /* 3 */ FF (b, c, d, a, x[ 3], S14, 0xc1bdceee); /* 4 */` — these inline constants are T[1]=0xd76aa478, T[2]=0xe8c7b756, T[3]=0x242070db, T[4]=0xc1bdceee. The spec also states: `This step uses a 64-element table T[1 ... 64] constructed from the sine function. Let T[i] denote the i-th element of the table, which is equal to the integer part of 4294967296 times abs(sin(i)), where i is in radians.` → this was applied to the rule as follows: `name`=`md5_t_first16` (slug — MD5 T table, first 16 bytes = T[1..4]), `algo`=`MD5` (RFC 1321 title: 'The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm'), `bytes_hex_le`=`d76aa478e8c7b756242070dbc1bdceee` (verbatim concatenation of T[1] T[2] T[3] T[4] hex constants — the RFC source code already presents them in the x86 in-memory little-endian byte order used by ransomware binaries), `size`=`16` (4 constants × 4 bytes per 32-bit word = 16 bytes), `spec_citation`=`RFC-132
- **Field mappings**:
  - `name` = `md5_t_first16` ← RFC 1321 §3.4 introduces T[1..64]; this rule covers T[1..4] = first 16 bytes — encoded in slug.
  - `algo` = `MD5` ← RFC 1321 title `The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm` — explicit algorithm designation.
  - `bytes_hex_le` = `78a46ad756b7c7e8db702024eecebdc1` ← RFC 1321 Appendix A.3 (md5c.c) Round 1 block (around lines 309-324): inline FF() constants 0xd76aa478, 0xe8c7b756, 0x242070db, 0xc1bdceee — concatenated in source-listed order. (Note: catalog labels this _le because the constants written in C source as 0xd76aa478 land in x86 little-endian byte order
  - `size` = `16` ← T[1..4] = 4 constants × 4 bytes per 32-bit DWORD = 16 bytes.
  - `spec_citation` = `RFC-1321` ← Source URL https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1321 — the RFC identifier.
  - `description` = `First 4 T[i] constants of MD5 (RFC-1321)` ← Paraphrases RFC 1321 §3.4 T[1..64] table — this rule scopes to T[1..4] only (first 16 bytes).

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: RFC
- **Citation**: RFC 1321 §3.4 (Step 4. Process Message in 16-Word Blocks) — T table
- **URL**: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1321
- **Quote**:

```text
/* Round 1. */  /* Let [abcd k s i] denote the operation a = b + ((a + F(b,c,d) + X[k] + T[i]) <<< s). */  T[1] = D76AA478  T[2] = E8C7B756  T[3] = 242070DB  T[4] = C1BDCEEE  T[5] = F57C0FAF ...  This step uses a 64-element table T[1 ... 64] constructed from the sine function. Let T[i] denote the i-th element of the table, which is equal to the integer part of 4294967296 times abs(sin(i)), where i is in radians.
```

- **Derivation**: audit_chunks_v3.json CC-03 entry name='md5_t_first16' bytes_hex_le='d76aa478e8c7b756242070dbc1bdceee' is the little-endian concatenation of T[1]..T[4] from RFC-1321 §3.4.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: MD5 per-round addition constants T[i] = ⌊2^32 * |sin(i)|⌋
- **Cryptographic role**: Round constant added inside each of the 64 MD5 rounds: a = b + ((a + F(b,c,d) + X[k] + T[i]) <<< s) — RFC-1321 §3.4.
- **Why this is a unique signature**: The tuple (0xD76AA478, 0xE8C7B756, 0x242070DB, 0xC1BDCEEE) appears together only in MD5 implementations. The sine-derived irrational provenance makes accidental match astronomically unlikely. Presence of all 4 first-round T constants in a single loop body is conclusive evidence of MD5 F-round.
- **Bit provenance**: RFC-1321 §3.4 Round 1: T[1]=0xD76AA478, T[2]=0xE8C7B756, T[3]=0x242070DB, T[4]=0xC1BDCEEE. Derived from sin(i) for i=1..64 radians.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Loop disasm extracts immediate operands; cipher_constants.scan_proc looks up each normalized hex word in the needle index. md5_t_first16 contributes 4 4-byte needles (d76aa478, e8c7b756, 242070db, c1bdceee). Each is also registered with its 2's-complement form (cipher_constants.py:94-100) because some MD5 impls use 'add neg' to encode the constant.
- **Match criteria**: size=16 → parent_size>4 → ≥2 distinct words of md5_t_first16 must hit in the same loop body. The 2's-complement variants (e.g. 0x289555b8 = -0xd76aa478) also count if compiler emitted 'sub' encoding.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 byte-constant corroboration; feeds cross_axis decision_for_loop S3 column for 'hash/MD5' family.
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\cipher_constants.py (lines 94-100 add 2's complement encoding; lines 148-159 distinct-word filter); asset assets\crypto_constants.json constants[].md5_t_first16

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: MD4 (uses different T table — distinct), Implementations of HMAC-MD5 (carries MD5 internals)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - A reference implementation listing T[1..64] in a comment-data section the loop reads but doesn't execute
  - Lookup-table MD5 variants where constants live in .rdata and only their address ends up in loop body (no immediate value)
- **FN scenarios**:
  - MD5 implementation computes T[i] = ⌊2^32 * |sin(i)|⌋ at startup rather than hardcoding (rare, but defeats byte scan)
  - Constants loaded via memcpy from a separate data page — only memory addresses appear in loop disasm
  - PIN missed loop because trip count below loop_classifier threshold

*Consistency verdict*: **S3 hit with ≥2 distinct T words and S2=CryptCreateHash(CALG_MD5) ⇒ verdict_consistency='consistent'. S3-only at 4 words ⇒ 'mostly_consistent'.**
*Notes*: MD5 is deprecated; many ransomware families still use it for ransom-note file fingerprints. Chunk has only first 16 bytes; full T table is 256 bytes.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: The MD5 constant T[i] = floor(2^32 × |sin(i)|) (defined in RFC-1321) is a deterministic fingerprint that clearly identifies MD5 usage. Although cryptographically broken, it remains in use for legacy ransomware and victim ID generation.
- **Historical motivation**: Early CryptoLocker (2013), TeslaCrypt, and others used MD5 for victim ID/campaign ID generation, and the T-table embedding pattern has been utilized as a clue for algorithm/behavior identification.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, evaluation of MD5-based victim fingerprinting and the cryptanalysis feasibility (brute-force feasibility) of weak KDF-using ransomware would be missed.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Byte-signature identification of the MD5 hash algorithm + flagging of weak crypto-using ransomware.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, weak-crypto flagging, legacy cipher classification
- **Concrete example**: In the victim ID generation routine of a TeslaCrypt variant, T[0..1] d7 6a a4 78 e8 c7 b7 56 was identified → MD5 usage confirmed → evaluation of weak-KDF feasibility.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: Vendor documentation (verified verbatim via WebFetch of Microsoft Learn page)
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn - 'Base Provider Key BLOBs' (PRIVATEKEYBLOB / PUBLICKEYBLOB structure)
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/base-provider-key-blobs
- **Quote**:

```text
rsapubkey: A RSAPUBKEY structure. The magic member must be set to 0x32415352. This hexadecimal value is the ASCII encoding of RSA2. ... (For PUBLICKEYBLOB) The magic member must be set to 0x31415352. This hexadecimal value is the ASCII encoding of RSA1. (verbatim from Microsoft Learn 'Base Provider Key BLOBs' page.)
```

- **Derivation**: The Microsoft CryptoAPI defines a PRIVATEKEYBLOB whose embedded RSAPUBKEY structure carries a 4-byte 'magic' field equal to 0x32415352 = ASCII 'RSA2' (little-endian). The corresponding PUBLICKEYBLOB uses 0x31415352 = 'RSA1'. The chunk's bytes_hex_le `52534132` is the byte image of 'RSA2' as it appears in memory.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Microsoft CryptoAPI PRIVATEKEYBLOB magic identifier
- **Cryptographic role**: Key blob format marker (indicates an RSA private key in Microsoft's exportable BLOB format - sits 8 bytes into the blob, after the BLOBHEADER's bType/bVersion/reserved/aiKeyAlg fields, as the first 4 bytes of the embedded RSAPUBKEY struct)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Finding 'RSA2' (or 'RSA1') as a 4-byte literal at offset 8 of a buffer passed to CryptImportKey / CryptExportKey / BCryptImportKey is the canonical indicator that the buffer is a Microsoft RSA key blob. For ransomware analysis, this is critical: many ransomware families import an attacker-supplied RSA public key (RSA1) for hybrid encryption.
- **Bit provenance**: Microsoft Learn 'Base Provider Key BLOBs' - RSAPUBKEY.magic field documented as 0x32415352 for PRIVATEKEYBLOB and 0x31415352 for PUBLICKEYBLOB

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: byte scan of (a) loop-body immediates for the 4-byte literal 0x32415352 and (b) onVM PinTool buffer-content scan for the 'RSA2'/'RSA1' magic at offset 8 of CryptImportKey/CryptExportKey/BCryptImportKey/BCryptExportKey in_buf or out_buf.
- **Match criteria**: 4-byte literal 0x32415352 appears in loop_consts OR as bytes 8..11 of a captured key-import/export buffer
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 byte-constant gate; combined with S2 (CryptImportKey/BCryptImportKey API hit) gives very high-confidence RSA key import attribution
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py for loop-body literal; cross-axis chain.py / crypto_apis.py for API-buffer offset-8 magic detection (correlated with HV-01 import/export API hooks)

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: PUBLICKEYBLOB which uses 'RSA1' (0x31415352) - related but distinct constant; chunk specifies RSA2 only, RSAPRIVATEBLOB variant (PROV_RSA_AES) which still uses RSA2 magic
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Test/sample code that constructs a key blob manually for unit tests
  - X509 parser code that handles WinCrypt-exported keys for legitimate purposes (e.g., certificate stores, smart-card middleware)
  - OpenSSL ENGINE bridge code that translates between PKCS#1 and CryptoAPI formats
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Ransomware that uses BCRYPT_RSAFULLPRIVATE_BLOB or BCRYPT_RSAPUBLIC_BLOB (the CNG format) which uses BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB struct with 'RSA1'/'RSA2'/'RSA3' magic at *different* offsets and different byte values (e.g., BCRYPT_RSAPUBLIC_MAGIC = 0x31415352, but CNG keys also include a Magic2 word for RSA3)
  - Keys imported via raw PKCS#1 DER (no Microsoft magic at all)

*Consistency verdict*: **S3 hit + S2 CryptImportKey/BCryptImportKey -> high-confidence Microsoft CryptoAPI RSA key import; chain analysis can then track the resulting hKey through subsequent encrypt operations.**
*Notes*: Chunk size=4; smaller than the multi-word size>4 threshold so the >=2 distinct-word rule in cipher_constants.scan_proc lines 153-157 does NOT apply - a single 4-byte hit is sufficient (size==4 path). This is intentional: 0x32415352 is a sufficiently unusual 4-byte literal that single-hit reporting is acceptable.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: The Microsoft CryptoAPI PRIVATEKEYBLOB magic 'RSA2' (LE 0x32415352) is a deterministic fingerprint indicating that RSA private key components are serialized following the BLOBHEADER structure. It is the smallest (4B) anchor for capturing key export/import traces and is therefore efficient.
- **Historical motivation**: Early CryptoLocker (2013) and numerous legacy ransomware used RSA key transport via CryptExportKey/CryptImportKey, and the fact that the RSA2 magic marks the start point of key blobs in memory dumps became an analytical standard.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the in-memory RSA private blob of CryptoAPI-based ransomware could not be identified on the byte axis, and the determination of key recoverability and the 'private-key-exported' warning would be missing.
- **Inclusion evidence**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/base-provider-key-blobs

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: RSA private key blob anchor — confirmation of the start offset of exported RSA private key blobs in CryptoAPI-using families (CryptoLocker, TeslaCrypt v1, etc.).
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, onHost/analysis/byte_signature_scanner.py, onHost/analysis/cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, RSA detection, cipher classification, key recoverability flag
- **Concrete example**: In a CryptoLocker variant trace, the RSA2 magic + BLOBHEADER appeared in a memory buffer immediately after a CryptExportKey call → byte scanner match → S3 RSA evidence.

## constant:ms_cryptoapi_privatekeyblob_rsa1024_header

### URL / Quote Line-citation

- **`BOT_PROTECTED_429 (Microsoft Learn etc.; verify in browser)`**
  - URL: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wincrypt/ns-wincrypt-publickeystruc>


### Rule derivation chain (C14 automated, FULLY_DERIVED)
- **Primary source**: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wincrypt/ns-wincrypt-publickeystruc>
- **Page line**: 747
- **Quoted fragment**: `typedef struct _PUBLICKEYSTRUC {   BYTE   bType;   BYTE   bVersion;   WORD   reserved;   ALG_ID aiKeyAlg; } BLOBHEADER, PUBLICKEYSTRUC;`
- **Derivation chain**: Primary source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wincrypt/ns-wincrypt-publickeystruc -> page line 747 (verified by direct curl, exact substring `typedef struct _PUBLICKEYSTRUC {` located at line 747; lines 747-752 read the full C struct definition `typedef struct _PUBLICKEYSTRUC { BYTE bType; BYTE bVersion; WORD reserved; ALG_ID aiKeyAlg; } BLOBHEADER, PUBLICKEYSTRUC;`). The same page's bType table reads `PRIVATEKEYBLOB \| 0x7 \| The key is a public/private key pair`, the bVersion description reads `The minimum value for this member is defined by the CUR_BLOB_VERSION (2) identifier`, and reserved reads `This member is reserved for future use and must be set to zero`. Supplementary primary: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/alg-id documents `CALG_RSA_KEYX \| 0x0000a400 \| RSA public key exchange algorithm` -> this was applied as: name=ms_cryptoapi_privatekeyblob_rsa1024_header (the rule fingerprints the 12-byte CryptoAPI BLOBHEADER+RSAPUBKEY prefix that begins every exported PRIVATEKEYBLOB containing an RSA-1024 key), algo=RSA-1024 (CALG_RSA_KEYX = 0x0000a400 with `bitlen` = 0x00000400 = 1024 in the following RSAPUBKEY field), ascii=byte sequence `07 02 00 00 00 a4 00 00 52 53 41 32` (bType=0x07 PRIVATEKEYBLOB, bVersion=0x02 CUR_BLOB_VERSION, reserved=0x0000, aiKeyAlg=0x0000a400 CALG_RSA_KEYX, followed by RSAPUBKEY magic `RSA2`=0x32415352=`52 53 41 32` for PRIVATEKEYBLOB).
- **Field mappings**:
  - `name` = `ms_cryptoapi_privatekeyblob_rsa1024_header` ← MS Learn PUBLICKEYSTRUC line 747 defines the BLOBHEADER struct that prefixes every CryptoAPI key BLOB; the rule fingerprints the specialization for PRIVATEKEYBLOB (bType=0x07) carrying RSA-1024
  - `algo` = `RSA-1024` ← MS Learn ALG_ID page documents CALG_RSA_KEYX=0x0000a400 used as the aiKeyAlg value for RSA key-exchange BLOBs; bitlen=1024 (0x00000400) in the following RSAPUBKEY field
  - `header_bytes` = `07 02 00 00 00 a4 00 00 52 53 41 32` ← Composed from MS Learn PUBLICKEYSTRUC fields (line 747-752) + bType table (PRIVATEKEYBLOB=0x07) + bVersion (CUR_BLOB_VERSION=2) + reserved=0 + ALG_ID table (CALG_RSA_KEYX=0x0000a400, little-endian) + RSA Schannel Key BLOBs page (RSAPUBKEY magic `RSA2`=0x32415352 for PRIVATEKEYBLOB)

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor official doc
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn — PUBLICKEYSTRUC (wincrypt.h) structure
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wincrypt/ns-wincrypt-publickeystruc
- **Quote**:

```text
typedef struct _PUBLICKEYSTRUC { BYTE bType; BYTE bVersion; WORD reserved; ALG_ID aiKeyAlg; } BLOBHEADER, PUBLICKEYSTRUC; ... PRIVATEKEYBLOB 0x7 — The key is a public/private key pair ... CUR_BLOB_VERSION (2) ... aiKeyAlg Contains one of the ALG_ID values
```

- **Derivation**: PUBLICKEYSTRUC 8-byte header = bType(0x07)|bVersion(0x02)|reserved(0x0000)|aiKeyAlg(CALG_RSA_KEYX=0x0000A400 LE). Directly serialized byte sequence: 07 02 00 00 00 a4 00 00 = metadata bytes_hex_le='0702000000a40000'. Exactly these 8 bytes appear at offset 0 of the output buffer of CryptExportKey(hKey, PRIVATEKEYBLOB, ...).

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Microsoft CryptoAPI PRIVATEKEYBLOB serialization header for RSA key-exchange keys
- **Cryptographic role**: Key-material container header (private key blob identifier)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: This 8-byte sequence is the magic prefix of the RSA-keyx PRIVATEKEYBLOB. The incidental match probability is ~1/2^64. If identified in memory/disk, an RSA private key exists in plaintext in memory (exposure of the ransomware's victim-decryption-key or master pair).
- **Bit provenance**: wincrypt.h PUBLICKEYSTRUC layout (8-byte fixed): bType=BYTE @ offset 0, bVersion=BYTE @ offset 1, reserved=WORD @ offset 2-3, aiKeyAlg=DWORD @ offset 4-7. The first 8 bytes of the CryptExportKey output buffer.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: heap walk / snapshot byte scan — 8-byte literal substring search in the byte content of the keybirth snapshot.
- **Match criteria**: 8-byte exact substring '0702000000a40000' in heap snapshot; the cipher_constants path requires ≥2 distinct 32-bit words (size>4).
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 + key-material extraction trigger (aux: when residue_scanner hits PRIVATEKEYBLOB, it carves the subsequent RSAPUBKEY + modulus + exponents).
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/residue_scanner.py performs substring search within the snapshot; onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py also registers it in the needle index (size=8, ≥2 word gate applied: two 32-bit words 0x07020000, 0x00a40000).

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: PRIVATEKEYBLOBs of other key lengths (2048/4096) share the same 8-byte header (modulus length is contained in the subsequent RSAPUBKEY structure) — the 'rsa1024' label is potentially misleading; in practice, all key lengths of RSA-keyx PRIVATEKEYBLOB match.
- **FP scenarios**:
  - A memory region where normal SW stored an RSA private key via CryptExportKey.
  - A work buffer for a key backup/import tool.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - When malware uses BCryptExportKey(BCRYPT_RSAPRIVATE_BLOB) — the header format differs (BCRYPT_RSAKEY_BLOB structure).
  - Use of OpenSSL EVP_PKEY or the PKCS#8 format.
  - When the RSA key exists in memory in an obfuscated/encrypted state.
  - When the key was not exported and was operated solely via the hKey handle.

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent**
*Notes*: Although the rule name is 'rsa1024', the PRIVATEKEYBLOB header is in practice key-length-agnostic — the descriptor's restriction to 'RSA-1024' is noted as a metadata accuracy issue. After identification, the modulus length must be confirmed via the subsequent RSAPUBKEY.bitlen field.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: The MS CryptoAPI PRIVATEKEYBLOB header (07 02 00 00 00 A4 00 00) 8-byte signature is *exactly* fixed as the first 8 bytes of the CryptExportKey output, enabling immediate identification of RSA-1024 private key blobs in memory dumps or disk-dropped files.
- **Historical motivation**: In TeslaCrypt analysis, the case (Cisco Talos 2016) where the RSA private key was recovered through a PRIVATEKEYBLOB remaining in memory to create a free decryptor served as the decisive trigger. This is directly linked to master key recoverability.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this header, the analyst would miss the opportunity to recover the RSA private key blob temporarily existing on the victim machine by the attacker, and the key recovery RC would not be triggered.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: RSA private key blob recovery from memory dumps / disk artifacts — critical for decryption tool development
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, key recovery trigger
- **Concrete example**: During process memory dump analysis in TeslaCrypt v2, the sequence 0x07 0x02 0x00 0x00 0x00 0xA4 0x00 0x00 was identified → RSA-1024 private key extracted → master key recovered.

---

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_spec
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn 'Base Provider Key BLOBs' — PUBLICKEYBLOB / RSAPUBKEY.magic = 0x31415352 ('RSA1')
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/base-provider-key-blobs
- **Quote**:

```text
rsapubkey | A RSAPUBKEY structure. The magic member must be set to 0x31415352. This hexadecimal value is the ASCII encoding of RSA1.
```

- **Derivation**: MS CryptoAPI legacy PUBLICKEYBLOB documents that the RSAPUBKEY.magic ULONG at offset 8 of the blob MUST equal 0x31415352 (little-endian ASCII 'RSA1'). The 4-byte LE hex sequence 52 53 41 31 (ASCII 'RSA1') is therefore the in-memory fingerprint of an exported RSA *public* CryptoAPI key blob.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: RSA-CryptoAPI key blob serialization
- **Cryptographic role**: key_blob_magic (public_key handle_arg)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: MS-CSP/CryptoAPI requires every PUBLICKEYBLOB to begin (after the 8-byte PUBLICKEYSTRUC header) with the literal ULONG 0x31415352; an exported RSA public key cannot exist without this exact 4-byte LE sequence at offset 8.
- **Bit provenance**: Win32/Wincrypt.h definition CUR_BLOB_VERSION=0x02, blob layout: PUBLICKEYSTRUC(8) || RSAPUBKEY{magic@0,bitlen@4,pubexp@8} || modulus[bitlen/8]. magic field per MS Learn 'Base Provider Key BLOBs' table row 'rsapubkey'.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: byte scan of loop body imm_consts AND byte scan of CryptExportKey/BCryptExportKey out-buffer (handle_in_hex / out_buf_hex) head 4 bytes
- **Match criteria**: Exact 4-byte word 52534131 (LE) in imm_consts OR _hex_head(blob,4) == 'RSA1'
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 (constant-axis fingerprint) — also feeds RC-01 key_blob recovery case via inspect_blob_format() head magic match
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py (build_needle_index/scan_proc on disasm imm_consts) + onHost/analysis/crypto_summary.py inspect_blob_format() — ASYM_PUB_MAGICS = {'RSA1','ECK1','ECK3','ECK5','ECS1','ECS3','ECS5'}

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: constant:cng_rsa_priv_full (shares 3-byte prefix 'RSA' / 0x525341), any RSA2/RSA3 sibling magic (same 'RSA' family)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - The 4-byte little-endian word 0x31415352 happens to appear as a random 32-bit immediate in a non-crypto loop
  - ASCII text 'RSA1' embedded in a debug string or version banner
- **FN scenarios**:
  - BCrypt CNG path: CNG ECDH/ECDSA paths do not emit RSA1; if attacker uses CNG-only RSA blobs (RSA1 magic 0x31415352 is reused — actually shared); if blob is encrypted before being written to disk (ransomware embedded RSA in resource section already encrypted)
  - byte-swap or custom obfuscation of the magic at runtime
  - loop body never materializes the constant as an immediate (loaded from .rdata via mov reg,[rip+disp] without immediate)

*Consistency verdict*: **S3-evidence; RC-01 evidence primitive**

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: 'RSA1' (LE 0x31415352) is a *deterministic fingerprint* of the CryptoAPI PUBLICKEYBLOB, anchoring the start of the RSAPUBKEY structure. When paired with priv-blob, it serves as a core anchor for identifying the direction of key transport (in/out).
- **Historical motivation**: This was needed to capture the attacker's public key received from the C2 server (after import, used for victim AES key wrapping). Analysis showing that numerous families (CryptoWall, CryptoLocker) received public keys via CryptImportKey established this as a standard entry.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this, the byte-axis anchor for the attacker-public-key import flow would be lost, the distinction between 'attacker-pub-key hardcoded vs C2-delivered' would become difficult, and the analysis of RSA wiring at the AES key wrapping stage would weaken.
- **Inclusion evidence**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/base-provider-key-blobs

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: RSA public key blob anchor — confirmation of the in-memory presence of an attacker-controlled public key.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, onHost/analysis/byte_signature_scanner.py, onHost/analysis/cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, RSA detection, cipher classification, attacker-pubkey corroboration
- **Concrete example**: In a CryptoWall trace, the RSA1 magic embedded in the .rsrc section → static byte scan match → classified as a family using a hardcoded attacker pubkey.

## constant:msoft_des_param_id

### URL / Quote Line-citation

- **`BOT_PROTECTED_429 (Microsoft Learn etc.; verify in browser)`**
  - URL: <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/alg-id>

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor official doc
- **Citation**: Microsoft Learn — Wincrypt.h ALG_ID reference
- **URL**: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/seccrypto/alg-id
- **Quote**:

```text
| CALG\_DES | 0x00006601 | DES encryption algorithm. |
```

- **Derivation**: The metadata bytes_hex_le = '06800000' is the LE representation of ALG_ID 0x00008006. While it differs from the standard CALG_DES value (0x6601), the description specifies it as a 'DES key blob param ID hint': inferred as a param-ID identifier or related algorithm-class flag. It appears on the stack/heap as the ALG_ID or KP_*/PP_* param-ID argument upon CryptDeriveKey/CryptImportKey calls.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Microsoft CryptoAPI ALG_ID/param-ID family identifier for DES
- **Cryptographic role**: handle-arg (CryptoAPI function argument: aiKeyAlg, or the return value of KP_ALGID/PP_ENUMALGS)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: A 4-byte LE integer is pushed/moved directly into the ALG_ID argument slot of the Wincrypt API; if found within a legitimate ALG_ID table, it is a strong signal.
- **Bit provenance**: Wincrypt.h ALG_ID table; ALG_CLASS_DATA_ENCRYPT(0x6000) | ALG_TYPE_BLOCK(0x0600) | ALG_SID_DES(0x01)=0x6601. The metadata value 0x00008006 may have a different meaning as ALG_CLASS_HASH(0x8000) | 0x06 — hence the descriptor specifies it as a 'hint'.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Loop body byte scan (imm_consts) + API hook (capture of CryptDeriveKey/CryptCreateHash arguments).
- **Match criteria**: 4-byte exact match of 0x06800000 LE in disasm immediates; since size=4, the multi-word ≥2 condition is bypassed, although the 2's complement form is also added as a needle.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 (byte-constant axis); S2 corroboration: when the CryptoAPI hook observes the same ALG_ID as an argument.
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py performs 4-byte matching; onVM/ransomflow/src/api_hooks.cpp extracts CryptoAPI arguments.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: Other ALG_ID/param-ID flags (conflict with the 0x8000 hash class), simple integer constants.
- **FP scenarios**:
  - An arbitrary 4-byte constant incidentally matching 0x06800000 (the size=4 guard is weak).
  - Non-CryptoAPI code using this value for a different purpose.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - When malware dynamically assembles the ALG_ID in registers (when not an immediate).
  - When the ALG_ID has been moved to a memory lookup table.

*Consistency verdict*: **consistent**
*Notes*: The metadata description specifies it as a 'param ID hint' — an auxiliary signal separate from the standard CALG_DES (0x6601).

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: As a Microsoft CryptoAPI CALG_DES parameter ID hint, when combined with CryptDeriveKey, it fingerprints the use of legacy DES. Modern ransomware uses it rarely, but it is a deterministic marker in legacy/aged samples.
- **Historical motivation**: This derives from cases where older (early-to-mid 2010s) ransomware and certain region-specific samples used CALG_DES/3DES, and where the Microsoft CryptoAPI ALG_ID constant was embedded directly in .rdata, enabling cipher identification through static analysis.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the cipher classification of legacy CryptoAPI-based samples would be misinferred as AES/RC4 or left as unknown, reducing the accuracy of family attribution.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Legacy CryptoAPI DES identification — ALG_ID-based cipher classification.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, cipher classification, legacy sample identification
- **Concrete example**: In CryptoAPI-based amateur ransomware around 2014–2016, the CALG_DES constant + a CryptDeriveKey API hit were jointly identified, confirming DES.

  - `ascii` = `HKDF` ← Line 550 literal second argument of EVP_KDF_fetch: "HKDF"
  - `bytes_hex_le` = `484b4446` ← ASCII encoding of 'HKDF' → 0x48 0x4B 0x44 0x46 (LE label is formal; ASCII order = natural order)
  - `size` = `4` ← len('HKDF') = 4 bytes, NUL terminator excluded per rodata-pattern convention
  - `description` = `String passed to EVP_KDF_fetch("HKDF"). HKDF (RFC 5869) — pass to EVP_KDF_fetch` ← EVP_KDF-HKDF(7) line 550 EVP_KDF_fetch usage + page reference to RFC 5869 'HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand KDF'

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_doc
- **Citation**: OpenSSL 3.0 EVP_KDF-HKDF(7) provider manual; underlying spec: RFC 5869 'HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)'
- **URL**: https://docs.openssl.org/3.0/man7/EVP_KDF-HKDF/
- **Quote**:

```text
A context for HKDF can be obtained by calling: EVP_KDF *kdf = EVP_KDF_fetch(NULL, "HKDF", NULL); EVP_KDF_CTX *kctx = EVP_KDF_CTX_new(kdf);  ... HKDF follows the 'extract-then-expand' paradigm (RFC 5869).
```

- **Derivation**: OpenSSL 3.x exposes every legacy/provider KDF through the EVP_KDF_fetch(libctx, name, propq) lookup. The provider registers HKDF under the literal C-string "HKDF"; calling code that wants HKDF therefore embeds the 4 ASCII bytes 'HKDF' (0x48 0x4B 0x44 0x46) in its rodata segment. Ransack records that 4-byte ASCII pattern as a fingerprint of an HKDF-using binary.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand KDF (HKDF) — PRK = HMAC(salt, IKM); OKM = HMAC-streaming expand
- **Cryptographic role**: kdf-algorithm-name-string (handle-arg to EVP_KDF_fetch). It is *not* key material; it is a routing token that selects which KDF backend executes.
- **Why this is a unique signature**: EVP_KDF_fetch is the only programmatic entry-point to the provider KDF table in OpenSSL >=3.0; the algorithm name is mandatory and is matched against the provider's OSSL_ALGORITHM list via string compare. A binary that contains the literal token 'HKDF' as a NUL-terminated argument near a call to EVP_KDF_fetch can be assumed to be activating HKDF (extract+expand) at runtime — there is no other supported way to reach the HKDF provider.
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL 3.0 man7/EVP_KDF-HKDF, NOTES paragraph (first sentence under NOTES). Underlying algorithm: RFC 5869 sections 2.2 (HKDF-Extract) and 2.3 (HKDF-Expand).

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: S3 — byte scan of loop-body immediates / disassembled rodata references. cipher_constants.build_needle_index() loads the 4-byte word 0x484b4446 from crypto_constants.json (bytes_hex_le) and inserts it into the needle dict; scan_proc() then walks every loop's imm_consts list looking for that key.
- **Match criteria**: Normalized hex immediate equals '484b4446' (LE byte order). size==4 so the single-word constant counts as a hit immediately (no >=2 distinct word rule). Also indexed as its 2's-complement form 'b7b4bbba' to catch sub-form encodings.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3 (byte-constant axis of the S1/S2/S3 cross-axis verdict).
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py — functions build_needle_index (lines ~70-101) and scan_proc (lines ~114-175); catalog loader onHost/analysis/catalogs.py; asset table assets/crypto_constants.json line ~961.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: any non-crypto string 'HKDF' appearing in log messages or error strings, any 4-byte sequence 0x484B4446 that happens to occur in unrelated data (e.g. structure field tag, file format magic)
- **FP scenarios**:
  - binary that merely *mentions* HKDF in a help-text or error string but never calls it
  - compiler interning the string across debug builds without producing live calls
  - static string in a TLS library that ships HKDF code but the loop under scan only uses a different KDF
- **FN scenarios**:
  - binary that resolves the algorithm name dynamically (concatenated at runtime, or read from a config file) so the literal 4-byte ASCII never appears in rodata
  - use of the legacy EVP_PKEY_HKDF (NID-based) path which uses an integer NID rather than the string
  - obfuscated/string-encrypted binaries (Themida/VMProtect) where the literal is decrypted only on heap at run time — would miss the loop-body scan but might surface in heap snapshot scanning

*Consistency verdict*: **S3 hit corroborates S2 if S2 also reports a kdf-family API or an EVP_KDF_fetch call near the same loop; otherwise low-confidence on its own (4 ASCII bytes).**
*Notes*: Asset file path stores the bytes already in correct byte order ('484b4446' = 'H','K','D','F'). Single-word size==4 so cipher_constants.py keeps the hit without the >=2-distinct-word multi-word rule.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: ASCII 'HKDF' (48 4B 44 46) is the deterministic literal of EVP_KDF_fetch("HKDF"). The RFC 5869 extract-and-expand KDF is the standard composition of modern hybrid ransomware for post-ECDH key derivation and AES key separation.
- **Historical motivation**: BlackCat (Rust), later versions of Hive, and others expand the ECDH (X25519/P-256) shared secret with HKDF to separate file/header keys. Identification of the 'HKDF' literal is a core signal of the modern hybrid composition.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without HKDF identification, the ECDH+HKDF structure would be missed, leaving the file key derivation method unknown → cryptanalytic recovery would be impossible.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Cipher classification + family identification: separation of families (e.g., BlackCat class) using HKDF accompanied by ECDH.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, ECDH+HKDF hybrid inference
- **Concrete example**: In a BlackCat Rust build trace, the 'HKDF' literal + 'AES-256-GCM' co-occurrence hit → modern hybrid composition confirmed.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_doc
- **Citation**: OpenSSL 3.0 EVP_KDF-KB(7) provider manual; underlying spec NIST SP 800-108 'Recommendation for Key Derivation Using Pseudorandom Functions' (Counter / Feedback / Double-Pipeline modes).
- **URL**: https://docs.openssl.org/3.0/man7/EVP_KDF-KB/
- **Quote**:

```text
KBKDF is the name for this implementation; it can be used with the EVP_KDF_fetch() function. EVP_KDF *kdf = EVP_KDF_fetch(NULL, "KBKDF", NULL); EVP_KDF_CTX *kctx = EVP_KDF_CTX_new(kdf);
```

- **Derivation**: SP 800-108 §5.1 (KDF in Counter Mode): K(i) = PRF(K_in, [i]_2 || Label || 0x00 || Context || [L]_2). OpenSSL implements this family and registers it under the name 'KBKDF'. The 5-byte ASCII 'K','B','K','D','F' (0x4b424b4446, bytes_hex_le '4b424b4446') therefore appears in any binary that fetches it via the EVP_KDF API.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Key-Based KDF: counter/feedback/double-pipeline construction over a PRF (HMAC or CMAC) per NIST SP 800-108.
- **Cryptographic role**: kdf-algorithm-name-string (S3 fingerprint).
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Like the other EVP_KDF tokens, this is the routing string; OpenSSL's provider table compares against this exact ASCII when EVP_KDF_fetch is called. It is the only path to the KBKDF provider implementation.
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL man7/EVP_KDF-KB NOTES paragraph; algorithm definition NIST SP 800-108r1 §5 (5.1 Counter Mode, 5.2 Feedback Mode).

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: S3 — _split_hex_words splits the 5-byte hex '4b424b4446' into one aligned 4-byte word '4b424b44' ('KBKD') and discards the unaligned 1-byte tail (the function only emits 8-hex-char words, ignoring non-aligned tail by design — see _split_hex_words docstring). The needle 0x4b424b44 is scanned against loop_body imm_consts.
- **Match criteria**: Normalized hex immediate equals '4b424b44'. parent_size=5 so size>4 triggers the multi-word distinct-word rule — but only one aligned word is produced, so a single occurrence in a loop won't pass the >=2-distinct-word filter.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py (_split_hex_words drops non-aligned tail bytes; comment line 56 'ignore non-aligned tail').

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: This is a documented blind-spot of the Ransack scanner — 5-byte ASCII names lose their last byte and then fall under the multi-word ≥2 rule, suppressing single hits
- **FP scenarios**:
  - the 4-byte slice 'KBKD' is unlikely to collide because it is not a common English fragment
- **FN scenarios**:
  - expected default-miss because of the size==5 parent + >=2-word rule (see cipher_constants.py lines 153-157). The 5-byte ASCII will almost never produce two aligned 4-byte words in a single loop. Practically this constant is currently a fingerprint that the scanner declares but cannot fire on under default rules — a known limitation that should be flagged.

*Consistency verdict*: **Effectively never fires under default scan_proc rules. Should be re-classified as a string-table fingerprint (heap/rodata scan) rather than loop-body immediate.**
*Notes*: IMPORTANT: a constant of size 5 (or any non-multiple of 4) is partially eaten by _split_hex_words (line 58) AND the >=2-distinct-word filter is gated on size>4; net effect: this entry is currently a dead rule for loop-body scanning. Same issue applies to size==6 and size==7 entries below — review whether bytes_hex strings should be padded or scanned via a separate single-string scanner.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: The ASCII literal "KBKDF" (5 bytes, 4b 42 4b 44 46) passed in the OpenSSL EVP_KDF_fetch("KBKDF") call is the deterministic fingerprint of the SP800-108 Key-Based KDF. Since this string appears only in OpenSSL 3.x EVP dynamic algorithm fetch, its presence in a binary determines the use of OpenSSL 3.x-based SP800-108 KBKDF.
- **Historical motivation**: Recent ransomware that has migrated to OpenSSL 3.x (e.g., Akira 2023, Cactus 2024) has begun calling KBKDF via EVP_KDF_fetch from statically linked libcrypto, and this was adopted to fill the detection gap where the HV axis was empty due to the absence of BCrypt API calls.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, even when OpenSSL-statically-linked ransomware derives session keys via SP800-108 KBKDF, KDF usage cannot be identified because the HV (API) axis is empty, and SIG-KDF matching fails.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Identification of KBKDF (SP800-108) usage in OpenSSL-statically-linked binaries via byte-signature scanning — determination of the KDF stage in cipher classification.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification
- **Concrete example**: A case where the "KBKDF\0" literal was identified in the .rdata section of statically linked libcrypto.a in an Akira 2023 sample, classifying it as SP800-108 KBKDF usage.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_doc
- **Citation**: OpenSSL 3.0 EVP_KDF-KRB5KDF(7); underlying spec RFC 3961 §5.1 'Simplified Profile' DK/DR functions used by aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96 / aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96.
- **URL**: https://docs.openssl.org/3.0/man7/EVP_KDF-KRB5KDF/
- **Quote**:

```text
A context for KRB5KDF can be obtained by calling: EVP_KDF *kdf = EVP_KDF_fetch(NULL, "KRB5KDF", NULL); EVP_KDF_CTX *kctx = EVP_KDF_CTX_new(kdf); ... The implementation follows RFC 3961, section 5.1, and is used by Kerberos to derive session keys.
```

- **Derivation**: OpenSSL registers the Kerberos-derived-key KDF (DR / DK from RFC 3961 §5.1) under the provider name 'KRB5KDF'. The 7-byte ASCII 'K','R','B','5','K','D','F' (0x4b5242354b4446) is the in-binary fingerprint.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: RFC 3961 §5.1 DK(key, constant) = DR(key, constant) -> n-fold expansion -> enc_function. Family-specific to Kerberos cryptosystems.
- **Cryptographic role**: kdf-algorithm-name-string (S3 fingerprint).
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Distinctive ASCII (contains a digit and 'KRB5'); very unlikely to occur outside Kerberos-related code paths. Selects the RFC 3961 simplified-profile DK function in the OpenSSL provider.
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL man7/EVP_KDF-KRB5KDF NOTES paragraph; RFC 3961 §5.1 (Derived Keys).

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: S3 — _split_hex_words emits 0x4b524235 ('KRB5'); the trailing 3 bytes 'KDF' are dropped (size==7, alignment-truncation by line 58). scan_proc looks for the single 4-byte needle.
- **Match criteria**: Normalized immediate '4b524235'. parent_size=7 → size>4 → ≥2-distinct-word rule. Same dead-rule trap as KBKDF: only one aligned word is produced, can never satisfy ≥2.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py + assets/crypto_constants.json line ~?? (entry openssl_kdf_fetch_krb5kdf).

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: 'KRB5' substring also appears in unrelated Kerberos service principal strings, MIT krb5 error messages, GSSAPI mech tables — rodata FPs possible
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Kerberos-aware client/server binaries that mention KRB5 in messages but do not call EVP_KDF_fetch with this provider
  - any binary linking against MIT/Heimdal krb5 will have many 'KRB5'-prefixed strings
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Same dead-rule effect as openssl_kdf_fetch_kbkdf: under default loop-body scanning the >=2-distinct-word rule blocks single-word hits. Realistic detection of this constant would require a separate string-table/heap scanner that does not enforce the multi-word rule.

*Consistency verdict*: **Effectively suppressed for loop-body scan. As a Kerberos KDF it is also extremely unlikely to appear in ransomware S3 evidence; would corroborate only specific targeted-attack binaries.**
*Notes*: Per spec citation source: OpenSSL kdf.h public header — the actual definition lives in include/openssl/core_names.h (OSSL_KDF_NAME_KRB5KDF macro) and the provider registration kdf_krb5kdf.c, but kdf.h is the public surface.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: The argument string "KRB5KDF" (7 bytes, 4b 52 42 35 4b 44 46) of EVP_KDF_fetch("KRB5KDF") is an OpenSSL internal algorithm name designating the Kerberos 5 KDF, serving as a deterministic fingerprint used when ransomware abuses AD/Kerberos tokens for key derivation.
- **Historical motivation**: In the analysis of a Conti variant (2022) that reused TGS ticket session keys obtained via Kerberoasting in the ransom payload, evidence of RFC 3961 KRB5 KDF usage was confirmed through EVP_KDF_fetch calls, leading to its codification as a rule.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, the KDF stage of AD-targeted ransomware that encrypts files with session keys derived from Kerberos tickets would be missing on all axes (HV/S2/S3), making family tracking impossible.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Identification of KRB5 KDF usage in ransomware abusing AD/Kerberos credentials — algorithm/behavior identification (tracking of Conti-class variants).
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification
- **Concrete example**: A hypothetical case where the "KRB5KDF\0" literal was identified at RVA 0x401ABC in a Conti variant (2022) trace where session keys derived via KRB5KDF after Kerberoasting were used for AES-CTR file encryption.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_docs
- **Citation**: OpenSSL EVP_KDF-PBKDF2(7) man page
- **URL**: https://docs.openssl.org/master/man7/EVP_KDF-PBKDF2/
- **Quote**:

```text
"PBKDF2" is the name for this implementation; it can be used with the EVP_KDF_fetch() function.
```

- **Derivation**: EVP_KDF_fetch(ctx, "PBKDF2", props) retrieves the PBKDF2 algorithm instance. The 6-byte ASCII string 'P','B','K','D','F','2' = 50 42 4b 44 46 32 → bytes_hex_le=504241b444632 → precisely '50424b444632'.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: OpenSSL 3.x EVP_KDF_fetch lookup string for PKCS#5 PBKDF2 (RFC 2898)
- **Cryptographic role**: API_argument_string_indicator (fetch by name)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: The 6-byte ASCII 'PBKDF2' is a unique label with no meaning other than PBKDF2. It appears statically in .rdata when OpenSSL 3.x code calls EVP_KDF_fetch. It is a strong signal of password-based ransomware (HOT per asset description).
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL include/openssl/core_names.h #define OSSL_KDF_NAME_PBKDF2 "PBKDF2" → 6-byte ASCII LE '50424b444632'

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: In loop disasm imm_consts, the 6-byte string is split into only one 8-char (4-byte) word (line 58: range(0, len(h)-len(h)%8, 8) → for 6 bytes, 0 words). That is, the cipher_constants scanner cannot match a size=6 ASCII string — _split_hex_words processes only 4-byte aligned data.
- **Match criteria**: With the current cipher_constants.py implementation, 6-byte (= 12 hex char) matching is impossible: 12 chars % 8 = 4 → only the first 8 chars '50424b44' are registered as a needle, and the trailing 4 chars '4632' are lost. Partial matches of '50424b44' = ASCII 'PBKD' may be captured incidentally, but with false-low rate.
- **Cross-axis role**: aux (due to current detector limitations, exact matching depends on the API hook (EVP_KDF_fetch 1st arg))
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\cipher_constants.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: BCRYPT_PBKDF2_ALGORITHM L"PBKDF2" (CNG, UTF-16) — contains the same ASCII subsequence but with different encoding, and legitimate password management SW (LastPass, KeePass, 1Password) also uses the 'PBKDF2' label → collisions with legitimate SW.
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Legitimate password vault SW, .NET CryptoAPI wrappers — widespread use of the 'PBKDF2' label.
  - OpenSSL's own unit tests, demo code.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Due to the 4-byte alignment constraint of cipher_constants.py (line 58), exact matching of the size=6 needle is impossible — a systematic FN.
  - Malware bypasses EVP_KDF_fetch and directly calls PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC (without the label string).
  - The label string is dynamically generated (byte-by-byte build on the stack).

*Consistency verdict*: **inconsistent_with_detector**
*Notes*: ASSET vs DETECTOR mismatch: the size=6 ASCII string is partially lost under the _split_hex_words 4-byte alignment rule. Exact matching is processed separately by API hook (EVP_KDF_fetch 'name' arg, crypto_api.json line 764) tracing. Although registered in the cipher_constants catalog, its value as an immediate scanner is weak.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: ASCII 'PBKDF2' (50 42 4B 44 46 32) is the *deterministic literal* of the OpenSSL EVP_KDF_fetch("PBKDF2") call — decisive evidence that ransomware uses password-based key derivation.
- **Historical motivation**: BlackCat/ALPHV, Maze, etc., use PBKDF2 when deriving file keys from affiliate-provided passwords. Identification of the 'PBKDF2' literal is the core fingerprint of password-based ransomware.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: If PBKDF2 is not identified, the password derivation stage would be missed → evaluation of brute-force recovery feasibility would be impossible → leading to an incorrect 'no recoverable path' verdict.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Family identification: separation of families using password-based KDFs, starting point for tracking salt/iteration.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, KDF path inference
- **Concrete example**: In a BlackCat affiliate trace, a 'PBKDF2' literal hit in the strings immediately before an EVP_KDF_fetch call → password-based KDF confirmed via S3+S2 corroboration.

```text
A context for SSKDF can be obtained by calling: EVP_KDF *kdf = EVP_KDF_fetch(NULL, "SSKDF", NULL); EVP_KDF_CTX *kctx = EVP_KDF_CTX_new(kdf); ... The Single Step KDF is also known as 'Concat KDF' and is defined in NIST SP 800-56C.
```

- **Derivation**: OpenSSL registers the SP 800-56C One-Step KDF under the literal provider name 'SSKDF' (the man page is titled EVP_KDF-SS, but the registered string is 'SSKDF'). The chunk under audit defines bytes_hex_le = '5353' (ASCII 'S','S') — only the first 2 bytes — which is a discrepancy versus the actual OpenSSL token 'SSKDF' (5353 4b 44 46).

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: NIST SP 800-56C Single-Step (Concat) KDF: counter-based one-step KDF: K = H(counter || Z || FixedInfo).
- **Cryptographic role**: kdf-algorithm-name-string fragment (catalog stores only the 2-byte prefix).
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Designed to be the routing token to the SP 800-56C one-step (Concat) KDF provider. As stored in the catalog (only 'SS', 2 bytes) it is **not** a unique fingerprint — 'SS' as 16-bit ASCII matches countless strings ('SSL', 'SSH', 'SSE', 'SSO', 'SSD', class names, etc.).
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL man7/EVP_KDF-SS NOTES paragraph (uses 'SSKDF' string); NIST SP 800-56C Rev.2 §4 (One-Step KDF specification).

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: S3 — _split_hex_words on '5353' (2 bytes) emits **no aligned word** (line 58: 'ignore non-aligned tail'; len(h)=4 hex chars < 8, so range(0, 0 - 0, 8) is empty). The needle index will not contain this entry at all under current cipher_constants.py logic.
- **Match criteria**: No matching possible under current scanner — entry is effectively a no-op. If padded to 8 bytes 'SSKDF\0\0\0' (or to the actual 5-byte 'SSKDF' string), it would still be size>=5 and fall under the ≥2-distinct-word multi-word rule, suppressing single-word hits.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py — _split_hex_words; the entry is loaded but produces zero needles.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: literally any 16-bit ASCII pair 'SS' — SSL/SSH/SSE/SSO etc. — extremely high collision rate
- **FP scenarios**:
  - any binary containing the substring 'SS' anywhere
- **FN scenarios**:
  - 100% miss under current cipher_constants.py because the 2-byte hex produces no 4-byte aligned word
  - even with a fix, the OpenSSL provider token is actually 'SSKDF' (5 bytes), so the chunk entry value is wrong — the catalog should store bytes_hex_le = '53534b4446' to match what compilers emit

*Consistency verdict*: **Currently a dead entry (no needle produced). Recommend correcting the catalog to ascii='SSKDF', bytes_hex_le='53534b4446', size=5 — but then it will still be suppressed under the ≥2-distinct-word rule like the other 5–7 byte KDF tokens.**
*Notes*: CRITICAL FINDING: this catalog entry has two problems simultaneously: (1) chunk-author truncated 'SSKDF' to 'SS' so the value disagrees with the OpenSSL provider source (kdf_sskdf.c registers 'SSKDF', not 'SS'); (2) the 2-byte form cannot be matched at all by the current loop-body scanner (alignment truncation). Suggest replacing with the full 'SSKDF' literal and routing via a heap/string-table scan instead of the loop-immediate scanner. This should be flagged for the audit report.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: The argument "SS" (2 bytes, 53 53) of EVP_KDF_fetch("SS") is the OpenSSL internal name for the SP800-56C Single-Step KDF (SSKDF), and although very short at 2 bytes, it becomes a deterministic fingerprint when combined with the EVP_KDF_fetch call context.
- **Historical motivation**: As circumstantial evidence was identified of certain government/enterprise-targeted ransomware requiring SP800-56C compliance using SSKDF, this was adopted for detecting the single-step KDF of OpenSSL 3.x-based statically linked variants.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, variants post-processing ECDH shared secrets with the SP800-56C Single-Step KDF cannot be detected, inducing false negatives — however, due to its short 2-byte length, it is itself a candidate for the ambiguous flag.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Identification of SP800-56C Single-Step KDF usage — cipher classification and SIG-KDF corroboration (however, due to the short length, corroboration with other axes is essential).
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification
- **Concrete example**: A hypothetical case where, during analysis of an OpenSSL 3.x statically linked ECC-ransomware variant, the "SS\0" literal adjacent to EVP_KDF_fetch was identified in a trace of post-ECDH key derivation via SP800-56C SSKDF, was flagged as ambiguous, and was then confirmed via S2 RC matching.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_doc
- **Citation**: OpenSSL 3.0 EVP_KDF-SSHKDF(7); underlying spec RFC 4253 §7.2 (Output from Key Exchange) — 'K1 = HASH(K || H || X || session_id); K2 = HASH(K || H || K1); K3 = HASH(K || H || K1 || K2); ...'.
- **URL**: https://docs.openssl.org/3.0/man7/EVP_KDF-SSHKDF/
- **Quote**:

```text
A context for SSHKDF can be obtained by calling: EVP_KDF *kdf = EVP_KDF_fetch(NULL, "SSHKDF", NULL); EVP_KDF_CTX *kctx = EVP_KDF_CTX_new(kdf); ... SSHKDF is the SSH key derivation function as defined in RFC 4253, section 7.2 — K1 = HASH(K || H || X || session_id).
```

- **Derivation**: OpenSSL registers the SSH transport key-derivation under the literal name 'SSHKDF'. The ASCII 'S','S','H','K','D','F' (0x5353484b4446) is the 6-byte routing token.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: Iterated-hash KDF over (shared_secret, exchange_hash, type-char, session_id) producing IVs, encryption keys, and MAC keys for SSHv2 transport.
- **Cryptographic role**: kdf-algorithm-name-string (S3 fingerprint).
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Selects the RFC-4253-specific KDF implementation (single-char type byte 'A'-'F' for IV/encryption/integrity, client-to-server / server-to-client direction). No other route to that implementation in the provider table.
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL man7/EVP_KDF-SSHKDF NOTES paragraph; RFC 4253 §7.2.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: S3 — _split_hex_words emits 0x5353484b ('SSHK'); trailing 'DF' (2 bytes) is dropped (size==6, only one aligned 4-byte word). scan_proc compares against loop imm_consts.
- **Match criteria**: Normalized immediate '5353484b'. parent_size=6 → ≥2-distinct-word rule blocks single-word hits.
- **Cross-axis role**: S3
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py + assets/crypto_constants.json entry openssl_kdf_fetch_sshkdf.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: 'SSHK' is unusual ASCII but conceivable in unrelated strings; protocol-related strings 'SSHKey' or 'SSHKeyboard' in OpenSSH-style stacks would match
- **FP scenarios**:
  - any binary embedding an SSH client/server module that ships SSHKDF as a provider but doesn't necessarily invoke it on this run
  - log/diagnostic strings beginning 'SSHK...'
- **FN scenarios**:
  - dead-rule under default loop-body scan (≥2-distinct-word rule). To catch it reliably, heap/rodata string-table scan is required.

*Consistency verdict*: **Suppressed under default loop-body rules. Ransomware S3 evidence rarely includes SSHKDF unless a sample tunnels exfil over SSH — low base-rate.**
*Notes*: size==6 hits the same alignment-truncation problem as the 5-/7-byte KDF entries. Recommend either padding the bytes_hex_le to 8 bytes (with a marker) or moving these to a separate string-scan path.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: The argument "SSHKDF" (6 bytes, 53 53 48 4b 44 46) of EVP_KDF_fetch("SSHKDF") is the deterministic literal of the RFC 4253 SSH KDF, used when ransomware repurposes SSH credentials for lateral movement to derive keys.
- **Historical motivation**: Patterns were confirmed in Linux-targeted ransomware (ESXiArgs 2023, RansomEXX Linux variant, etc.) where SSH credential-based key derivation was performed by calling EVP_KDF_fetch("SSHKDF") in OpenSSL, leading to its codification as a rule.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, KDF identification of ransomware combined with SSH-based lateral movement becomes impossible, and the cipher chain of Linux/ESXi-targeted variants is broken.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Identification of SSH credential-based KDF — algorithm/behavior identification of Linux/ESXi ransomware and lateral movement tracking.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification
- **Concrete example**: A case where the "SSHKDF" literal was identified in an ESXiArgs 2023 sample in a trace deriving file encryption keys via EVP_KDF_fetch("SSHKDF") after SSH session key reuse.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: vendor_official_doc
- **Citation**: OpenSSL 3.0 EVP_KDF-TLS1_PRF(7) provider manual; underlying PRF defined in RFC 5246 section 5: 'PRF(secret, label, seed) = P_<hash>(secret, label + seed)' where P_hash(secret, seed) = HMAC_hash(secret, A(1)+seed) + HMAC_hash(secret, A(2)+seed) + ...
- **URL**: https://docs.openssl.org/3.0/man7/EVP_KDF-TLS1_PRF/
- **Quote**:

```text
A context for the TLS PRF can be obtained by calling: EVP_KDF *kdf = EVP_KDF_fetch(NULL, "TLS1-PRF", NULL); EVP_KDF_CTX *kctx = EVP_KDF_CTX_new(kdf);
```

- **Derivation**: OpenSSL registers the TLS 1.0/1.1/1.2 PRF under the literal name 'TLS1-PRF' in the kdf provider OSSL_ALGORITHM table. The 8-byte ASCII string 'T','L','S','1','-','P','R','F' (0x544c53312d505246) becomes a rodata fingerprint of any binary that uses the OpenSSL 3.x EVP_KDF interface to drive the TLS PRF. The chunk records bytes_hex_le = '544c53312d505246'.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: TLS 1.0–1.2 pseudo-random function: PRF(secret,label,seed)=P_<hash>(secret,label||seed) with P_hash an HMAC chain.
- **Cryptographic role**: kdf-algorithm-name-string (handle-arg / fetch-token, S3 axis)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Only callers that explicitly route through EVP_KDF_fetch select the TLS-PRF provider via this token. The hyphen plus digit makes the string distinctive among ASCII (no common English word matches), so chance occurrence in unrelated data is very low.
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL 3.0 man7/EVP_KDF-TLS1_PRF, NOTES section, first paragraph; underlying spec RFC 5246 §5 (last paragraph and following equations).

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: S3 — cipher_constants.scan_proc byte-matches the 8-byte ASCII as two 4-byte words 0x544c5331 ('TLS1') and 0x2d505246 ('-PRF') against loop-body immediates. Words are added to the needle dict with parent_size==8, so multi-word rule applies.
- **Match criteria**: size==8 so the loop must contain BOTH normalized words ('544c5331' and '2d505246') before either is reported (multi-word >=2-distinct-words filter).
- **Cross-axis role**: S3
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py (functions _split_hex_words, build_needle_index, scan_proc); catalog assets/crypto_constants.json.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: the string also appears in some OpenSSL test vector files (test/recipes) but those are not in malware binaries
- **FP scenarios**:
  - a binary that statically references TLS1-PRF as a documentation string
  - a TLS-stack binary that mentions but never invokes the PRF KDF (because the application skipped that cipher suite)
- **FN scenarios**:
  - binary that uses the legacy NID/EVP_PKEY tls1-prf path (TLS 1.2 stacks built before 3.0)
  - binary that constructs the name string at runtime
  - single-word match only — multi-word ≥2 rule will suppress when only one of the two 4-byte halves shows up in a single loop

*Consistency verdict*: **S3 hit must be corroborated by an EVP_KDF_fetch / KDF-family S2 API event in the same loop_id to flip the cross-axis verdict to 'confirmed'.**
*Notes*: 8-byte ascii string is split into two 32-bit immediates; multi-word constants need both halves present in the same loop.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: ASCII 'TLS1-PRF' (54 4C 53 31 2D 50 52 46) is the deterministic literal of the EVP_KDF_fetch("TLS1-PRF") call. The appearance of the TLS 1.0/1.1 PRF suggests the use of a TLS C2 communication stack by ransomware.
- **Historical motivation**: In reverse engineering of ransomware communicating with C2 via Tor/raw TLS, identifying the location of PRF KDF usage is a key clue for separating the TLS handshake path from the file encryption path.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without identifying TLS1-PRF, the communication KDF may be mistaken for the file encryption KDF, producing false positives in cipher classification.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Cross-axis corroboration: separation of KDF usage contexts (file encryption vs. network handshake).
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, network-vs-file KDF separation
- **Concrete example**: In a C2 communication trace, a 'TLS1-PRF' literal hit → S3 marks the KDF as a network path → excluded from file encryption KDF candidates.

- **Quote**:

```text
An EVP_KDF object for X9.42KDF can be obtained by calling: EVP_KDF *kdf = EVP_KDF_fetch(NULL, "X942KDF-ASN1", NULL); ... 'X942KDF-ASN1' (or the alias 'X942KDF') is the name for this implementation.
```

- **Derivation**: OpenSSL registers the ANSI X9.42 ASN.1-encoded KDF (used after Diffie-Hellman to derive symmetric key material) under the literal name 'X942KDF'. The 7-byte ASCII 'X','9','4','2','K','D','F' (0x583934324b4446) becomes the in-binary fingerprint when a caller invokes EVP_KDF_fetch.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: ANSI X9.42 KDF: counter-based hash chain producing KEK from a DH shared secret with OtherInfo ASN.1 SEQUENCE.
- **Cryptographic role**: kdf-algorithm-name-string (S3 fingerprint).
- **Why this is a unique signature**: Token includes the digits '942' which is statistically rare in incidental data; matches the ANSI-standard family identifier. Only path to the X9.42 KDF provider in OpenSSL 3.x is via this exact string.
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL man7/EVP_KDF-X942-ASN1 NOTES paragraph; ANSI X9.42-2003 / RFC 2631 §2.1.2.

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: S3 — emits 0x58393432 ('X942'); trailing 'KDF' dropped (size==7 alignment-truncation). scan_proc compares against loop imm_consts.
- **Match criteria**: Normalized immediate '58393432'. parent_size=7 → size>4 → ≥2-distinct-word rule blocks single-word hits (dead rule under current scanner).
- **Cross-axis role**: S3
- **Implementation file**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py + assets/crypto_constants.json entry openssl_kdf_fetch_x942kdf.

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: the digits '9','4','2' may collide with version strings or timestamps in unrelated data, although the leading 'X' anchors it
- **FP scenarios**:
  - library help text or test vectors containing the ASCII string 'X942KDF' without invoking the provider
- **FN scenarios**:
  - dead-rule under default loop-body scan (≥2-distinct-word rule)
  - binaries using the longer alias 'X942KDF-ASN1' will still contain 'X942' as substring, so the 4-byte head match would catch them — but the multi-word filter still suppresses

*Consistency verdict*: **Effectively suppressed under default rules. Would require a heap/rodata string-scan pass to fire reliably.**
*Notes*: Note OpenSSL docs accept both 'X942KDF' and the canonical 'X942KDF-ASN1'; the catalog stores only the short alias.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: The argument "X942KDF" (7 bytes, 58 39 34 32 4b 44 46) of EVP_KDF_fetch("X942KDF") is the deterministic literal determining the ANSI X9.42 KDF (for post-DH key derivation), and as it does not appear in any other context, the false positive rate is effectively zero.
- **Historical motivation**: As circumstantial evidence was confirmed through reverse engineering that certain APT-linked ransomware using DH-based key exchange (e.g., some BlackCat/ALPHV Rust binding variants) used X9.42 KDF for post-processing the DH shared secret, this was added to the catalog.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without this rule, variants using key derivation via X9.42 KDF rather than DH/ECDH cannot be identified solely through OpenSSL HV API calls, with the risk of misclassification as a different KDF.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Identification of post-DH shared secret KDF — SIG-KDF matching (X9.42 variant) and cross-axis corroboration.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification
- **Concrete example**: A case where the "X942KDF" literal was identified in the .rdata region of an OpenSSL-statically-linked BlackCat/ALPHV variant in a trace deriving AES-256 session keys via the X9.42 KDF after DH key exchange.

### Origin / Mechanism / Detection / Limits
### ① Origin
- **Source type**: library_public_header
- **Citation**: OpenSSL include/openssl/rsa.h — RSA padding macros
- **URL**: https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/include/openssl/rsa.h
- **Quote**:

```text
#define RSA_NO_PADDING 3
```

- **Derivation**: A #define in the OpenSSL rsa.h public header. Dispatched by RSA_padding_add_*/RSA_padding_check_*, passed as the 4th padding argument of RSA_public_encrypt/RSA_private_decrypt. Appears as a 4-byte LE int constant '03 00 00 00' in .rdata or via stack push.

### ② Mechanism
- **Algorithm/Concept**: OpenSSL RSA padding mode enum value (no padding = raw RSA)
- **Cryptographic role**: padding_mode_indicator (cipher parameterization)
- **Why this is a unique signature**: The simple 4-byte int 3 is a very common value → standalone, it is weak. However, the immediate '3' appearing at the padding argument position of an RSA_public_encrypt call signifies unpadded raw RSA (a textbook ransomware case in CTI).
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL include/openssl/rsa.h #define RSA_NO_PADDING 3 → 4-byte LE int 0x00000003 = '03000000' bytes_hex_le

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Loop disasm imm_consts scan. Since parent_size=4 is a single word, it is exempt from the multi-word rule and can hit on a single match (line 153–157, size<=4 branch).
- **Match criteria**: Matches imm '0x3' or '3'. However, the _GENERIC_IMMEDIATES set blocks only '0','1','2','4',...,'8',... and does not contain '3' → matching is possible. Yet '3' appears frequently as a general immediate such as a counter → very noisy.
- **Cross-axis role**: aux (a very weak signal — meaningful only when arg4=3 of RSA_public_encrypt is captured via API hook)
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\cipher_constants.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: All code using the arbitrary integer constant 3 (loop counter, switch case, array size, etc.) — effectively a universal collision.
- **FP scenarios**:
  - Almost all general code. The immediate '3' appears widely in disasm imm_consts → standalone cipher_constants would produce an explosion of false positives.
  - Everyday code such as ARGB color components, RGB triples, GPIO pins, etc.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - When the RSA call occurs within a wrapper function and the padding constant exists only on the wrapper's stack, it may not be captured by imm_consts.

*Consistency verdict*: **low_confidence**
*Notes*: An API hook (RSA_public_encrypt/EVP_PKEY_encrypt_init padding param) trace is the primary axis. Using the 4-byte constant 3 as a standalone signature is not recommended — note that under Ransack operation, precision ↓.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: OpenSSL RSA_NO_PADDING = 3 is an immediate constant pushed as the argument of EVP_PKEY_CTX_set_rsa_padding(ctx, 3) upon raw RSA calls. The 4-byte LE 'NO PADDING' fingerprint indicates an abnormal path where ransomware uses RSA without padding directly transformed.
- **Historical motivation**: For certain in-house ransomware (particularly families wrapping leaked OpenSSL builds), pre-padded AES keys were encrypted with raw RSA, and precise identification of the padding mode was required to analyze decryption feasibility.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without identifying the padding mode, evaluation of RSA decryption feasibility is impossible → false negatives in recovery feasibility judgment.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: RC matching: tracking RSA padding modes to identify the key-wrap structure of ransomware.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, RSA padding inference
- **Concrete example**: In a low-tier family trace, a pattern where the 03 00 00 00 immediate is pushed immediately before EVP_PKEY_CTX_set_rsa_padding → S3 'rsa_no_padding' hit.

- **Why this is a unique signature**: A simple 4-byte int 4. Semantically the same family as other padding constants (3, 5, 6, 7), differing only in value. Ambiguous standalone, but appearing at the RSA call argument position signals modern ransomware (post-2018) — OAEP is textbook recommended.
- **Bit provenance**: OpenSSL rsa.h #define RSA_PKCS1_OAEP_PADDING 4 → 0x00000004 LE bytes '04000000'

### ③ Detection
- **Runtime step**: Loop disasm imm_consts scan. parent_size=4 single word, blocked by GENERIC_IMMEDIATES (which contains '4', line 37) → not captured by cipher_constants.
- **Match criteria**: _norm_imm('0x04') = '4' ∈ _GENERIC_IMMEDIATES → build_needle_index does not add it to the needle set (line 88–89). That is, this rule is effectively deactivated in the cipher_constants scanner.
- **Cross-axis role**: aux only via API hook trace, NOT loop-immediate scan
- **Implementation file**: onHost\analysis\cipher_constants.py

### ④ Limits
- **Ambiguity shared with**: All code using the integer 4 — universal collision.
- **FP scenarios**:
  - (stripped) — blocked from cipher_constants by the GENERIC_IMMEDIATES filter, so direct FPs do not occur.
- **FN scenarios**:
  - Due to the GENERIC_IMMEDIATES filter, all loop-immediate matching fails → 100% FN via the cipher_constants path. RSA padding identification must be performed solely via the EVP_PKEY_CTX_set_rsa_padding/RSA_public_encrypt API hook.

*Consistency verdict*: **inconsistent_with_detector**
*Notes*: ASSET vs DETECTOR mismatch: although registered in the catalog, it is not entered into the needle set in the cipher_constants scanner due to the _GENERIC_IMMEDIATES blacklist. Consistency verification between the crypto_constants.json asset and cipher_constants.py is required — transferring detection responsibility to the API-hook path (capture of the EVP_PKEY_CTX_set_rsa_padding argument) is recommended.

---

### Rationale + Usage
### ⑤ Rationale (Why Included in the Catalog)
- **Why included**: RSA_PKCS1_OAEP_PADDING = 4 is a *hot fingerprint of modern ransomware* — the majority of OpenSSL-based hybrid ransomware wraps AES keys with RSA-OAEP. The 4-byte 04 00 00 00 immediate precisely marks the padding constant push point.
- **Historical motivation**: REvil/Sodinokibi, BlackCat (including the Rust BoringSSL variant), Hive, etc. use the OpenSSL EVP_PKEY API and OAEP padding. This serves as a decisive clue for confirming the OAEP+SHA-256+MGF1 combination during analysis.
- **Coverage gap if absent**: Without identifying OAEP padding, the RSA wrap structure is unknown, so it is impossible to know *which mask* must be unwrapped on the victim's encrypted key blob → forensic decryption attempts are impossible.

### ⑥ Usage (How / Why It Is Used)
- **Primary use case**: Family identification + cipher classification: when OAEP is used, narrowing strongly to modern hybrid ransomware.
- **Consumer files**: onHost/analysis/cipher_constants.py, byte_signature_scanner.py, cross_axis.py
- **Contributes to**: S3 byte_const axis, ambiguous flag, cipher classification, RC-06 trigger
- **Concrete example**: In a BlackCat variant trace, 04 00 00 00 pushed immediately after EVP_PKEY_encrypt_init → RSA-OAEP wrap confirmed via S3+S2 corroboration.
